speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ACT TO BE PROCLAIMED JULY 1 AND BECOME EFFECTIVE JANUARY 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, among the bills to which royal assent was given yesterday afternoon was the act respecting Canadian citizenship. The government has felt that hon. members would no doubt like to have this symbol of nationhood associated with the seventy-ninth anniversary of confederation, which comes on Monday next.
The government has therefore decided to have the bill proclaimed on July 1 of this year. I might say however that while the bill will be proclaimed on that day, its provisions will not go into effect until January 1, 1947. A number of technical matters have to be worked out in connection with the provisions of the bill, and as this cannot be done either here or in our offices abroad in that brief space of time, it has seemed appropriate to fix January 1, 1947, as the date upon which the provisions of the act will come into force.

subtopic: MR. MACKENZIE KING-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "FINANCIAL POST" OF JUNE 29

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. MACKENZIE KING-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "FINANCIAL POST" OF JUNE 29
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my attention has been drawn to an article appearing in the issue of the Financial Post, dated June 29, and which is headed, "Canada 'Another Belgium' in U.S. Air Bases Proposal? Hear Washington Insists Dominion's Northern Frontier be Fortified-'Atomic Age Maginot Line' is Feared". This wholly misleading article contains so many serious inaccuracies that I am bound to take exception to it in the strongest terms. Amongst other things the article alleges that a virtual ultimatum from the United States calling on Canada to fortify her northern frontier is reported to have hastened my return from England this month.
It- is, of course, absurd to imagine that the government of the United States would present anything that could, by any stretch of the imagination, be described as an ultimatum, and there is no foundation whatever for this allegation. It is also untrue, as claimed in the article, that the United States government has

Veterans Affairs-Women's Services
presented a plan for northern air bases. In view of what I have said, I perhaps need hardly add that my return from the United Kingdom was in no way influenced by any such imagined developments.
It is a fact, of course, that the permanent joint board on defence is charged with studying the defences of North America which includes our northern frontiers. The extent to which their vulnerability may or may not have been increased by reason of technological developments in recent years, and the measures which should be adopted for their protection are proper subjects of study by the board. The board is therefore examining them, and would be remiss in its duties if it did not.

speechtext: I was of the opinion that all the auxiliary services were to be brought within the scope of existing legislation for the benefit of veterans and that this matter is now in the hands of a subcommittee of the veterans affairs committee. I understood it was intended to bring in an all-inclusive bill to cover all auxiliary services. Why is it that this bill is introduced while the subcommittee is studying the matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
What the bon. member
has said is correct; the intention is to try to embody in one, bill whatever has to be done in regard to those who were not actually members of the armed services. However, these personnel are in a slightly different position. They were deemed to be members of the armed services until it was found that the South African military nursing service was not a part of the armed services of that country and because of that technicality the members of that service were not entitled to the benefits they would have been entitled to had they been members of the armed services. The hon. member will remember that last session the veterans affairs committee recommended that an order in council be passed giving them 
those rights, and it was of course understood that a bill would be introduced to embody those rights in legislation by parliament.
With regard to the women's royal naval service personnel, it was found that because of a naval rule of the United Kingdom these women could not be considered as members of the armed services as were the members of the women's auxiliary air force and the women's branch of the British army. These particular women therefore were not able to get the benefits of our legislation which extended to those who had joined His Majesty's forces other than Canadian, and the bill is to take care of this situation. As I explained at the resolution stage, it is the intention to try to get legislation before the committee and have a recommendation from the committee this session if possible in connection with the other groups not actually members of the armed forces.

speechtext: I am quite satisfied with the bill. speechtext: As chairman of the subcommittee which is considering other civilian personnel with respect to war service benefits, I should like to try to make it clear why these two groups are being considered now. The duty of the subcommittee is to recommend to the main committee such benefits as they can agree upon. There is no question at all of the others being ignored; their position has been considered and is being seriously considered, and in the course of time a report will be made to the main committee.

speechtext: Mr. W. A. TUCKER (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved the second reading of bill No. 199, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is good business to pass this bill in its present form. We have discussed this subject in the house for quite a number of years, and I think most of the members have admitted that we are not giving a square deal to our old veterans of the last war who settled on the land.
We had a discussion in the house in October last, in which more than twenty members took part, of a resolution to grant clear title to those who were settled on the land at the end of March, 1944, and only two or three members opposed that resolution. We are spending vast sums of money trying to be fair to people of other countries and improve their standard of living, and I think it would be very good business for us to begin at home. The amount required to grant clear title is $7,715,954.01. which is less than we spent on half a day of war. Divide the total up among the people of Canada andl it would mean an assessment of sixty-five cents each. After the budget news we had last night I do not think the people would be shocked if even at this late date we passed this bill with an amendment to give these old veterans at least something approaching a square deal. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden):
(a)	Striking out the word "sections" where it appears in the third line and substituting therefor the word "section."
(b)	Adding after the word "where" in the first line of the section the words, "on March 31 1944."
(c)	Striking out subsections (d) (e) and (f) of section 76.
(d)	Striking out section 77 and substituting the following as subsection (d):
_ "The government shall cancel all remaining indebtedness on account of the purchase agreement, and shall render to the persons so indebted full title to the said land," so that the bill will now read:
1. The Soldier Settlement Act, chapter one hundred and eighty-eight of the revised statutes of Canada; 1927, is amended by adding thereto the following section:
76. In any case where at March 31, 1944,
(a) a person is indebted in respect of any agreement made under this act;
Soldier Settlement

(b) a person has not abandoned his land;
(e)	the agreement has not been terminated, rescinded or assigned;
(d) the government shall cancel all remaining indebtedness on account of the purchase agreement. and shall render to the persons so indebted full title to the said land.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I suggest to Your Honour that the amendment is out of order in that it would impose a charge on the public revenue. Furthermore this is the first time that I have ever heard of a motion being made to amend a bill on the second reading. I submit that on both these grounds the amendment is not in accordance with the rules. My motion was that the bill he now read a second time. The effect of the amendment would be to substitute an entirely new bill altogether. It is in effect a negation of the motion for second reading. I submit that the amendment is out of order.

Speaking to the point of order, the first part of my hon. friend's argument may or may not be valid. The money that might be collected from the settlers would naturally come into the public revenue, but against that there is the charge of collecting the indebtedness, and it is conceivable that the cost of collection might easily equal the revenue received. The amendment if passed would bring justice to men who have been settled on their lands so long that they are now entitled to them. As to the second point, if you, Mr. Speaker, rule that this is the wrong place to move this amendment, we should be pleased to move it in committee of the whole.

On the point of order as to the amendment involving expenditure of money, that cannot possibly be so, because the money has not yet been collected to be spent, and all that is proposed in the amendment is to give clear title. If this were an amendment directly involving the expenditure of money-
You will save money on administration.
-I could understand it, but giving them a clear title does not involve the spending of money at all. They pay for the title themselves. They have paid already.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
If the hon. member who moved this amendment will look at Beauchesne, third edition, article 658, he will see that-
A motion opposing the second reading of a bill must not anticipate amendments which may be moved in committee. Alterations which may be effected by amending the clauses of the bill cannot be moved on the second reading.

So I declare that the amendment of the hon. member is out of order.
May I ask one question? Will it be in order to move the amendment in committee?

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: It will be the privilege of the hon. member to present his amendment when the house is in committee on the bill.

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Redirction of interest rate in case of a settler, veteran of two wars.

Mr. Chairman, since this resolution was considered the other day I have been looking up the records of the house in the last few years. I take it that the committee must be an impartial committee. I believed it was; I visited it the other day, but I was persuaded that there must be something else behind it. We know what happened after the last war when soldiers went on the land. I am not blaming now any one government, because it seems to me that as regards treatment of the soldiers they are all alike. That is one of the reasons I came here in the first place; I think I made a mistake in coming here at all. By way of contrast, consider what this country has done for the builders of the trans-Canada railways-the C.P.R., the C.N.R., the Grand Trunk Pacific-the Mackenzie and Mann system. What they received from this country, including the grants of land, the numerous sections along the lines of railway handed to them as a favour, without any consideration for the taxpayer at all, runs into millions of acres on the broken and unbroken rights of way of each.
Then consider what we have done for the builders of character over Canada from the time immemorial-the rural school teachers engaged to teach in our country schools, who are left to starve on $300 a year. Finally, consider how the soldiers have been treated. I have seen a good many ex-service men who were stationed during the war at the Canadian national exhibition grounds in Toronto. Large numbers of them were collected at a sort of central Canada concentration camp for the whole of the west and all Canada. These men came from as far east as Halifax and as far west as Vancouver. I have talked to them. Some came in to see me, some wrote me letters, some of the men who were in this plight served in the last war and some are veterans of this war. I consider that on the question of soldier settlement some of them have received pretty shabby treatment. I

Soldier Settlement
have the utmost respect for this committee of veterans and for the various governments which have had to deal with these problems, because we have to consider also the taxpayer, but I want to draw attention to the position of a large body of people who, except for what the minister did in 1945, which applied to only a few, have never got so much as a snap of the finger by way of consideration from any government since the time when, enrolled in the Northwest Field Force, 1885, they marched across lake Superior in the time of the Riel rebellion. Some of them were Haligonians; there was a large contingent from the midland district, from Trenton, and neighbouring cities and towns; there were the Royal Grenadiers, and in Toronto the Governor General's bodyguard, the battalion commanded by that great police magistrate, the late Colonel Denison, one of the pioneers of this country, the Queen's Own, and many other units.
Where are these men to-day? They never got a cent. I admit that they were given a grant of land which they never saw and was of no use to them. The soldier land settlement schemes began, in fact, at the time of the northwest rebellion in 1885. Some of these men received grants of land in the northwest; some, up in new Ontario, and half of them never saw their land. They were in their day the backbone of the present Canadian militia. They and their children served in the South African war and they or their children and grandchildren served in the two great wars which followed it. How were they treated? As to old age pensions they were subjected to the means test-and it is very well named; it is a mean thing; it is the meanest and most contemptible thing I have ever known. In connection with the case I mentioned the other day to the committee, what did they do? They simply did nothing, and I made up my mind that I would speak in this chamber when this particular bill came up, because if this is the way the veterans committee conducts its affairs, the remnant of these old soldiers-nearly all of them are gone now, I think there are only three or four thousand left-will get scant consideration. As a matter of fact they never got a nickel out of parliament. They never even received uniforms. All they got was $6 a year for attending drills in the militia, and they had to put the money, in 1881 and 1885, in the company funds. The way they have been treated since is shabby and contemptible.
I commend the action of the hon. member for Battle River. I do not often agree with some of the views of the hon. gentlemen of 63260-189
his group, but there is one thing to be said for them: they stand for the underdog and they support the mother country first, last and all the time; it is not with their consent that the Suez canal will be given away or India abandoned and the dominions separated from the empire.
I repeat that I am disappointed with the present bill. I believe it should be referred back to the committee to see if they cannot make a more liberal recommendation. I was surprised to some extent by what occurred when I attended a meeting of the committee the other day. They heard what I had to say; the chairman called me his "colleague," and I am a colleague of his. I have no antagonism to anybody. But I do repeat that these 1885 veterans have got shabby treatment from all the governments. I was accused away back in 1915, 1916 and 1917 of attacking my own party when it was in power, and I admit that when I saw the shabby treatment the veterans were getting I protested against the government of which I was a supporter. When I saw the disgraceful hospital conditions that prevailed at the time of the terrible influenza epidemic, when men were forced to live out in tents in cold and rainy weather. I attacked my own party, who were then in office. I know a good many of these land settlement soldiers; I come in contact with many of them every day, and I have yet to see a returned man who has made anything out of it.
The night before last there was a big parade of soldiers to the Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto. I was not there, because members of parliament from Toronto cannot very well be there and here at the same time. There was a tremendous torchlight procession, and the men were discussing the housing shortage for veterans, the very question that I am now dealing with. They had great banners and they marched up to the Maple Leaf Gardens where they hoisted their banners, and I saw a report in the newspapers that a Scottish aider-man, John Innes, and' acting Mayor McCallum and Controller McKellar were among those present. The member for Davenport was not able to be there but he was represented by another Scotsman, John Innes. Well, these men wanted to know what the government was going to do about a number of things. They wanted to know something about housing; they wanted to know what was going to be done for those who were coming home; they wanted to know what plans the government had for adequate hospitalization of the men, and for nurses. I am glad I did not have to answer for all this. They spoke the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth as to

Soldier Settlement

'conditions under which the veterans have to live to-day, and those conditions are certainly intolerable.
I am not blaming the chairman of the veterans affairs committee. I have linked up in the past all governments with the shameful treatment that has been handed out to our soldiers. I have known something about all the governments we have had; I have known some of them a long time, too long as a matter of fact; and I know that the soldiers get-nothing much out of them. Last June there was a gathering of veterans of the 1885 Northwest force from all parts of Canada, about 217 of them, many of them well up in years, and they came to Toronto for a final dinner. What did they get? Nothing. The committee before whom I appeared on June 11 have as yet not recommended anything for them. I know the reason, and some day I will state it very emphatically and clearly in this house. Some day, right in this chamber, I am going to tell why the veterans of the northwest rebellion never got any direct aid except a little under an order in council in 1944-45, for which few could qualify. I have seen their wives and children actually passing the hat. I am sorry to have to say this, but it is the truth. Why should this state of affairs go on when we have a. veterans affairs committee that might be doing something for the veterans?
When I visited the committee I was greatly surprised, and I could then, realize fully the truth of what has been said so often by two of the best soldiers of our country, two Victoria Cross men sitting here modestly, and raising their voices all the time on behalf of the veterans. I have no doubt that what they say is quite correct. I think the veterans committee ought to do something for these men, who went on the land after world war I, and for that reason I support the recommendation that has been made in regard to the quit claim deed-. I have listened to what has been said not only by members of the house and members of the committee but by those who support the government, and I am ready to admit that the government have done a great deal for the veterans in the way of pensions and in other directions. What they have done in that regard is laudable, and in some respects it leads other countries. I was in hopes therefore that when I went to the committee I would see them making an earnest effort to redress the grievances of the men. That is what the veterans affairs committee is for, to redress the grievances of veterans not only of this war, not only of the last war, but of every other war in which Canadians have fought for their country. The Canadian people do not expect this parliament to act simply as a dead-beat in relation to the men who gave

up everything and went overseas in the last war, or the men who took part in the Fenian raid, in the South African war and in the northwest rebellion. At that time they marched along the shore of lake Superior in the depth of winter to save that land from dislocation. They had to live on hard-tack, and they got nothing out of it. They bought their own uniforms and did not receive a nickel. The people are not going to put up with this sort of thing much longer. The government can vote a billion and a half in civil estimates. We all heard the speech delivered by the Minister of Finance last night. When we consider these things, it is about time that private members got up and spoke on behalf the just grievances of the soldiers.
I believe in the sincerity of the present minister, who has done so much, and that of the chairman of the committee. I have no doubt he washes to do the very best 'he can for the men, and so I suggest that the government reconsider the suggestion that has been made in regard to the veterans of the last war who went on the land. I admit what was -done for Mackenzie and Mann by the government that I supported, but the other government and this government did a great deal too. Those people got a hand-out from our various legislatures of millions of acres of land. They were well treated by the province of Manitoba and by other provinces. If the country can do so much for these people, why can we not do something for our own land settlement veterans? The committee would be well advised to reconsider the matter, and I hope that when the minister comes back he will take it into further consideration.

I wish to support what my colleague the member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has said concerning the bill. I trust that the member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) will press his amendment; for I certainly believe that these old soldiers should have further consideration. Speaking on the measure the other day I pointed out what had happened in my own community, where one settler agreed to pay $5,000 for a half section, which was subsequently sold to a man, not a British subject, for less than ten per cent of that figure, and the settler himself was not given an opportunity to repurchase the farm. I told of the excellent brief that had been presented by the executive of the old veterans to the veterans committee in the railway committee room this summer. At that time I questioned some of the officers, and in this morning's mail, as a result of that, I received a letter from one of the old settlers in which he states:

Soldier Settlement
During the recent visit I note that on page 381 of minutes of May 6 you asked Mr. Sibley, our secretary, if he knew of any case where the dollar for dollar was conceded to civilian repurchasers, some being German ex-servicemen who had fought against us.
The chairman will remember that they made this representation in their brief, and when I questioned the witness he said he was not sure, but it was his understanding. My correspondent writes further:
At the time I was down in 1944 I addressed the cabinet, Conservative and Liberal caucuses, and stated flatly that I could provide them with proof of its having been done right in my own district.
This settler was forced to sign a quit claim deed, and the board in turn sold the land to a German ex-serviceman who had fought against us and later had come to this country. Later over the year's when adjustments were made to settlers, granting them a credit of two dollars for every dollar paid, this German settler who had fought against us received the same consideration. He received this consideration because he had come to this country and purchased that settler's farm. This man gives the evidence in a letter, and he also says that he had made the statement publicly before officials of the government of the day. Surely our settlers are entitled to at least as much consideration from the government as German ex-servicemen.
Much has been said about the veterans committee. I do not know whether the public realizes just how difficult our task is at times, because the reestablishment of soldiers involves various departments of government. This morning I received a letter from one of my constituents. He encolsed a copy of a letter which he had received from the wartime prices and) trade board, sugar administrator. The letter reads as follows:
The Wartime Prices and Trade Board Sugar Administration,
Area Sugar Office Power Building,
Mr. E. A. Tate,	Winnipeg, Manitoba
Killarney, Man.
Dear Sir:
That part of your letter dated 12th June, with reference to sugar for use in curing of meats has been referred to this office for attention.
In reply, we would advise that since all industrial sugar users are rationed on a percentage of 1941 usage, during which time you were not in business, it is impossible for us to establish an industrial sugar quota for you.
We regret that present regulations do not allow any deviation from this policy.
This veteran served in the armed forces for between five and six years, four and a half years of which he served overseas. I have sent a copy of all this correspondence to the Minister of Finance under whose jurisdiction the wartime prices and trade board operates. I do not know whether I shall be permitted to 63260-1894
put on Hansard the language he uses in regard to the wartime prices and trade board, but I shall read the letter which he asked me to send to the proper authorities.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member carries out his threat I would ask you to consider whether it is pertinent to the bill now under discussion. The letter has to do with the administration of the wartime prices and trade board regulations.
On the point of order, this matter has to do with the reestablishment of veterans of the recent war.

Coming back to the main argument, may I say that relief should be given to that young man. I hope that the member for Battle River presses his amendment as indicated, and I shall support him at every opportunity.

There probably will be one in a few minutes. I realize that I am not permitted to anticipate. In view of the letter from one of these old settlers, which I read, and the financial consideration that the taxpayers of this country have given to the German veteran who fought against these old soldiers and who came to this country later, I say that these old soldiers are entitled to some further consideration. I do not think there is any doubt about that. I do not know why there is a concerted effort on the part of the government to dispose of this matter as they are attempting to do at this time. If we are to consider-I was going to say-almost squandering huge sums of the taxpayers' money in every direction, why should we be so niggardly toward these old soldiers? It was they and their dependents who made it possible for us to enjoy our present way of life in Canada. We should give them some further consideration at this time and thereby enhance the welfare and the future of this nation.

At first I had not intended to take any part in the discussion, but I must confess I was greatly impressed by the remarks made by the hon. member for
[The Chairman.]
Battle River (Mr. Fair). They recall to my mind a case which I had before the house on two or three different occasions. It was that of a young soldier whose name I shall refer to as Lieutenant Frank M., of the county of Wellington, Ontario, who during the first great war won the military medal, and who later went to Saskatchewan and took up land. He was financed by his father, who at that time was financially well-off in Ontario. Later because of drought and depression this young man went through trying times. I received many letters from him at that time and I brought his case up in the house and pressed for relief to be given to him so that he might hold his land. I am sorry to say that in the end he signed a quit claim, deed and lost not only what he had put into the farm but what his father had put in. He then left that part of the country, and the father afterwards died.
After listening to the hon. member for Battle River present his plea I had hoped that the parliamentary assistant to the minister, who is doing a good job in piloting the bill through the house, would give some relief to these people. I do not suppose any relief can be given to the young man I mentioned, because he lost his land some time ago.

I shall send the particulars to him, to see if any relief can be given to this young man who lost everything he had in the world. As I said, he won a decoration in the last war. During the past war he acted as a guard in one of the prisoner of war camps at Lethbridge. What I started to say was this, that the parliamentary secretary is a westerner, sympathetic, and he is a former soldier. As such he must be thoroughly conversant with the trials and troubles through which many of these people passed during those terrible days of depression. I urge upon him that he use his influence with the minister, so that the minister may give a sympathetic ear to the submissions made by the hon. member for Battle River.

Mr. Chairman, I have sat as long as I can listening to hon. members on the other side of the house talking as though

Soldier Settlement
they were the only ones interested in veterans affairs. I do not like using the first person pronoun, and seldom do; but I served in the armed forces for six years, as did a good many others on this side of the house, as well as on the other side.
The veterans affairs committee has been coming in for a bit of battering, and I do not care for it. We have enough fighting among ourselves, because where one finds soldiers he generally finds fighting. Eventually they get together. But when it all has to be fought out again in the House of Commons, I resent it.
I resent, too, the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview, much as I respect his age and his great knowledge. He has been in parliament a long time. I saw him here over twenty years ago, when I was a small boy. We were good enough to allow him to come to our committee so that he might present his case. I was there at the time, and with the others listened with keen interest to what the hon. member had to say. The ideas he advanced were duly considered. But for the hon. member to come here and make the remarks he did about the veterans affairs committee is just a little too much, and I resent it.
I will tell you this, that I came back from the war, but I have not yet been able to get into business. I came to the House of Commons, telling my constituents that I was coming here to try to help the veterans. I am not a professional parliamentarian; that is obvious. But if this sort of thing continues I personally am going to resign from the veterans affairs committee, because I have heard accusations coming from the opposite side of the house which I strongly resent.
Here we have bill No. 199, which purports to do something for the veterans. I am not objecting to what the hon. member for Battle River has said. He has been fighting this matter for years, and fighting for what he believes is correct. I have no recrimination whatsoever to lodge against him; he is doing what he believes is right. I am not saying I think it is right; neither am I saying anything against the hon. member. That is another story. But I do maintain that this bill is going to help the veterans-that is, if we can get it through. So why not deal with what we have before us now? Get that through; and if there is anything else to be brought up, bring it up. It is obvious that the government is willing to put this measure into effect as soon as it can.
I know the hon. member for Battle River is in dead earnest in what he has said, and in the amendment he has said he will move. I know many other veterans think the same as he does. I am trying to be frank, because
I am not a politician. In my view the $5,000,000 item is not a very serious one. But I do feel that in view of what we might run into in the future, it would be a dangerous precedent to establish. We must remember that a great percentage of our national revenue is going to veterans and veterans affairs. We must keep the public in a state of mind in which they will favour supporting veterans affairs, and in which they will see that veterans get the best possible deal. The only way we can do that is to produce legislation which the public will think is fair, and which will leave them with the feeling that we are doing the right thing.
Mind you, I think the general public would probably favour what the hon. member for Battle River has said; but from what I have seen in parliament, if we start on a procedure of that kind it is apt to grow and grow. We may not feel the full effect of it at the present time. My view is, however, that in ten or fifteen years we will be going through harder trials than we are to-day, in connection with making readjustments and that sort of thing.
I may be wrong in that, of course; it is only my opinion.
I do suggest that in future we ought not to lose our tempers-as I did just now-but that we should forget about the veterans affairs committee as such in this debate. We are in there, trying to do a good job; do not criticize it. We are working hard all the time-I believe it is the hardest working committee in the House of Commons. Further, we will do our best-and if there is any political finagling it certainly is not all on one side, I can tell you that. Let us get on with the business, and try to get this bill through.

I thank the hon. member for the sympathetic and fair-minded view he has taken. I would also point out to him that so far as I am concerned I have no interest in politics. I have a much better home on the farm than I ever had here in Ottawa. I am quite satisfied that our climate in Alberta is much better than the climate here. So far as I am concerned I should be quite willing to . stay at home as soon as the people in my constituency think I have given them sufficient service. But realizing that forty-eight per cent of my constituents voted for me, from a field of five, I feel that what I have carried on in the past has been along the right line, and that they will want me to carry it through to a finish.
I assure the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare that I have no political interest at all, because I managed to make a living through the depression years, and did not have to come to Ottawa to get it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Rosthern has raised a question with regard to the contents of the letter the hon. member for Battle River is about to read. The fact that it has been considered in the committee does not prevent any member of the committee from bringing it up in the house.

This came up before the steering committee on two or three occasions and we felt that it would not do any good to allow the man who had written the letter to come down. It was thought that if we allowed individual cases to come before the committee we would never get through the business. The procedure in the veterans affairs committee has been not to deal with individual cases. That is why we did not take up this particular case. If that is according to the rules, then I think it should be brought to the attention of the hon. member.

I believe the members of the veterans affairs committee and the members of this committee are conversant with the case with which I was about to deal. I did not make a suggestion; I asked a question.

Having heard a little about this case perhaps 'hon. members will interest themselves in the particulars of it and try to learn about the kind of house this man is

living in, and what kind of bedding he has in the winter time, and whether he has to sleep in a fur coat in ordler to keep warm. They may then decide whether that is good enough treatment for a veteran of great war I. Having said that, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton:

Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Mr. Chairman, I
happen to be in the unfortunate position at this moment of leading the house on behalf of the government, and it is my responsibility to point out to you that this proposed amendment is absolutely unconstitutional. It is not a matter of order; it is a matter of attempting to do something which the constitution says cannot be done. Sections 53 and 54 of the British North America Act, by which we are all bound and which cannot be changed by any vote of this house, provide:
53.	Bills for appropriating any part of the public revenue or for imposing any tax or impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
54.	It shall not be lawful-
That is the constitution:
-for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the governor general in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or bill is proposed.
We all listened with very much interest, and with sympathy as well, to the arguments adduced at the resolution stage when it was suggested that it would be the proper thing for this country to forgive the indebtedness still due by the settlers under this Soldier Settlement Act. It was pointed out that it would
[Mr. Fair.l
amount to a little more than $5,000,000, and not more than that, as a direct remission, and that that was a small enough contribution to make for the relief of the veterans in question. But that is what this proposed amendment to the bill would do directly. It was pointed out in the course of debate that it would probably destroy the effectiveness of the administration of the Soldier Settlement Act at the present time if a sum, even if it be only $5,000,000, were forgiven at this time because it had not been paid at the moments when under the contracts it would have become payable. But that just cannot be done. Citation 549 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms says:
The rule-
That is the rule of the constitution :
The rule also applies to releasing or compounding any sum of money due to the crown and to the imposition of any state tax upon the people, but not to pecuniary penalties necessary to the operation of a bill.
I appreciate that there are many hon. members who wanted to have their views on the record as being favourable to the course proposed. But under the constitution as we have it, the house cannot do what is proposed unless there is brought into the house a resolution recommended by His Excellency the Governor General. That is the situation under the constitution. I submit to you, sir, that it is not a question of order. It is not a question of a standing order of the house that can be varied by the majority. It is a positive impediment-

Was this bill preceded by a message from His Excellency?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Oh, yes.

I do not recall it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There was a resolution recommended to the house- by the governor general and it was debated at considerable length In the course of that debate it was pointed out that the forgiving of this indebtedness would mean directly only $5,000,000 odd; that was the amount of indebtedness which those supporting that view would like to have the country give up. But the house cannot do it under our constitution until it is recommended to the house by His Excellency the Governor General.

Section 54 of the British North America Act refers to the appropriation of any part of the public revenue. Is this public revenue? What about the cost of collecting it?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The cost of the administration of the government of Canada frequently more than equals the revenue of the

Soldier Settlement
government of Canada, but that does not mean that what is collected is not a part of the revenue of Canada. That is an appropriation proposed of a part of what is due to become a portion of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.

It may be revenue in the future; it is not revenue now.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is an asset, for whatever it is worth, that belongs to the government of Canada, and that asset cannot be disposed of by the house without a message from His Excellency the Governor General recommending a resolution to that effect.

It just says revenue.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not going to
redraft it. I am submitting that it means that anything belonging to Canada cannot be disposed of without its disposal being recommended to the house by the governor general.

On the point of order I would point out that Hansard does not record a message from the governor general, either at the resolution stage, at page 2818 of Hansard, or on the first reading of the bill, at page 2868. In neither case was the house informed that the contents of the resolution or of the bill had been communicated to His Excellency and that His Excellency had approved its submission to the house. Is it the fact that His Excellency gave that permission before the resolution was introduced?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member will find that, in Votes and Proceedings. The practice is that notice of the intention to introduce a resolution is placed on Votes and Proceedings and there is a similar one on the Votes and Proceedings to-day. On the orders of the day it will be inscribed as a notice of government motion and it will be called and the Speaker will declare the minister moves that at the next sitting the house go into committee of the whole to consider the terms of the resolution, and at that moment the minister in charge of the resolution gets up and declares that the resolution has been, communicated to the governor general and that he is pleased to recommend it to the consideration of the house. Then next day or at some later day it is called to be considered in the committee. I will find for the hon. member the reference in the Votes and Proceedings to the declaration by the minister in charge that this was recommended to the consideration of the house.

I do not think the argument of the Minister of Justice is very strong. We have no proof, as far as I can see, that this 63260-190	[DOT]
is going to cost the country any money; in fact I think it would save the country money, and, what is more important, it would save a whole lot of suffering to the old veterans who fought in the first great world war.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Would the hon. member permit me to give the hon. member for Eglinton the reference? It has now been turned up. The consent of His Excellency the Governor General was communicated to the house by the Minister of Veterans Affairs on April 12 last; and that report is to be found at page 137 of the Votes and Proceedings of this session.

Carrying on, Mr, Chairman, 1 was trying to point out that there is a question of justice to these old veterans which has never been recognized during all this time. A concession has been made-I am quite willing to admit that-but I must also point out that the concessions never caught up with the disadvantages under which these men have worked all these years. I think we should take into consideration, as well as the legal aspect, some of the humanitarian considerations.
The second argument advanced by the Minister of Justice is that this proposal would destroy the administration of this particular board. I do not think that that is quite correct, because taking this as a precedent, a man settling under the Veterans Land Act cannot claim any such deal as w'e are proposing for the old veterans until twenty-five years after he has settled on his holding; and I hope that this country will not impose upon veterans of the last war conditions which will prevent them from paying their debt for a term of twenty-five years, because I think you all realize that a whole lot of suffering can be packed into twenty-five years, even when these people are in the prime of life.

Apparently under section 54 of the British North America Act it is not lawful for the house to pass any such resolution or bill for the appropriation of any tax or impost to any purpose that has not been first recommended to the house by a message of the governor general in the session in which the vote, resolution, address, or bill is proposed. I can assure hon. members that a recommendation will be asked for from the governor general, and that a request or resolution from the soldier settlers who are affected in this respect will be sent to the governor general from that organization. Whether he will act upon it or not I do not know. By this section, of course, the government itself must sponsor any such motion, and I appeal to the members of the government who have

Soldier Settlement

the interests and the welfare of these men at heart, to exert their influence along that line.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member for Battle River, in view of the remarks made by the Minister of Justice, is withdrawing his amendment?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Then it is necessary for me to consider the remarks which have been made by the Minister of Justice, and also by the hon. member for Battle River and the hon. member for Yorkton, with respect to this matter. The Minister of Justice has raised the question whether the amendment can be considered in the committee in accordance with the constitution. He has referred to the British North America Act, section 54. Before reading that section I shall read, not the whole of the proposed amendment, but the last clause, which states:
The government shall cancel all remaining indebtedness on account of the purchase agreement and shall render to the person so indebted full title to the said land.
Section 54 of the British North America Act reads:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address,, or hill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed.
Now I would refer hon. members to Beau-chesne's "Parliamentary Rules and Forms", third edition, paragraph 436, where it is stated:
The recommendation of the crown is needed for such measures as bills relating to the extension of time for the repayment of the deposit which has become liable to forfeiture in the case of a private bill;
And I would ask hon. members to note the following words:
the release or compounding of sums due to the crown;
This amendment proposes that there should be a release of certain sums due the crown. It would therefore appear that it would first have to have the approval of His Excellency the Governor General. If it has not that approval it would be beyond the powers of -even the government itself to make such an amendment, and I would say that the government itself could not advance a bill of this nature unless the government had first obtained the approval of the governor general.
Might I draw to the attention of hon. members a ruling which was made by the Hon. Mr. Lemieux on February 15, 1923, as
fMr. Casfleden.]
recorded in Beauehesne, 3rd edition, page 541. I will just read the headnote:
A resolution that the government relinquish certain specified claims cannot be considered on a private member's motion but must be taken up in committee of the whole upon the Governor General's recommendation.
It is necessary for me to consider whether or not this amendment comes within the powers of this committee; and I have come to the conclusion, after hearing the remarks of the hon. members to whom I referred a minute ago, that it is clearly not within our jurisdiction and that it is impossible for me to allow a question to be proposed upon the motion. Again I would refer to Beauehesne, 3rd edition, at page 168, where it is stated:
"If any motion, or bill, or proceeding is offered to be moved, whether in the house or in a committee, which requires, but fails to receive, the recommendation of the crown, it is the duty of the Chair to announce that no question can be proposed upon the motion . . ."
That is an extract from May, page 505.
And I see in Bourinot, at page 179:
In accordance with his duty he (the Speaker or Chairman) declines to submit to the house motions which obviously infringe the rules of the house or privileges of parliament, such as a motion which would create or increase a charge upon the people and is not recommended by the crown or a motion of which proper notice has not been given and in such case he shall apprise the house immediately as to the rule or authority applicable to the case.
I am therefore compelled to state that the amendment is obviously beyond the powers of the committee and I cannot propose it to the committee.
With all due respect, Mr. Chairman, I challenge your ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no appeal. I have not settled any point of order. It is my duty, before any amendment is considered in committee, to satisfy myself that it is within the jurisdiction of the committee. If I am of the opinion that it is not, there is no further debate upon it and there is no appeal. I would remind hon. members that standing order 12, section 1, provides that Mr. Speaker shall preserve order and decorum and shall decide questions of order, subject to appeal to the house without debate. enough, Mr. Chairman, to say under what standing order you take the view that although you have not declared the amendment out of order you stand on the constitution. I take it your ruling is that you have not declared the amendment out of order, but because in

235. Grant to Health League of Canada,

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
' Mr. BLACKMORE: There is one matter of great importance to the people of Canada as a whole which I should like to discuss for a few moments, and in order to do so properly I propose to begin by referring to the subject of cancer. This subject has been discussed by members on several occasions and it will do no 63260-1901
harm to review some of the facts pertaining to that dreadful disease.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
With all respect to the hon. member, I would raise the point that we are on item 235 which provides for a grant to the Health League of Canada.
I do not know of any way in which that grant is associated with cancer. When the estimates were under consideration before, on two separate occasions, we had lengthy discussions on cancer, and I would submit that, unless there is something in the hon. gentleman's remarks to show a greater relevancy than now appears, a discussion on cancer would not be in order on this vote.

Considering the fact that the health league is to-day engaged in a life and death struggle against cancer, above all things in Canada, the minister's remarks are astonishing. There is hardly an issue of the health league magazine that is not almost filled with discussions on cancer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I would submit that the time to discuss cancer is on something related to the general functions of the department, and not on a grant to the Health League of Canada. As part of its activities the Health League of Canada may do some educational work in connection with cancer, but I would submit that this discussion should have taken place when the administration of the department was under discussion and when we had a rather full discussion of the matter.
I presume that the publication of the health magazine is part of the activities of the Health League -of Canada. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes.
Very well. I am going to discuss one of the issues of the Health League of Canada's magazine.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I am not going to give a ruling definitely on the point raised, but I think all hon. members will agree that if we discuss cancer under the heading "Health League of Canada" we can probably discuss it again under practically all the items. The next item is "Canadian National Institute for the Blind". If cancer is discussed under the Health League of Canada it could be discussed under the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, or under the Victorian Order of Nurses, or the St. John Ambulance Association, and so forth. We did have a fairly general discussion on that subject when the estimates were before the committee previously. I ask the committee to endeavour to confine its dis-
Supply-Health and Welfare

cussion to the definite vote. The hon. member for Lethbridge saw something with respect to cancer in one of the magazines put out by the Health League of Canada. Of course he can discuss that.

I bow to your ruling quite readily, Mr. Chairman. Before I go on with the discussion I wish to suggest to the minister that this appropriation of $10,000 is either too much or it is not half enough. If the Health League of Canada is performing the function which hon. members of the committee would normally expect it to perform, then $10,000 is not nearly as much as it ought, to be given. If it is not performing that function we ought to cut down this appropriation to $100 or so. I think the Health League of Canada is performing, so far as it possibly can, the function which we would wish it to perform. If I am to be barred from the privilege of discussing the magazine- and I admit I am completely in the hands of the Chairman-then probably I shall have to find ways and means of accomplishing my objective without discussing canceir.
Let us take it for granted that the dreadful aspects of cancer are all known, and that its seriousness is well known. I wish to draw the committees attention to the fact that strange maladies are developing in our society, in Canada and in the United States. Men do not understand these maladies. The discussion on arthritis, which was carried on earnestly some time ago, indicates how completely bewildered the medical profession on the American continent is with respect to arthritis. The cause of cancer is, of course, completely unknown to us at the present time. Probably there is one thing which is standing in the way of our making effective efforts to discuss the nature and the causes of these maladies. I wish to give some attention to that to-day. There is an influence standing directly in the way of the discovery and introduction of adequate treatment of some of these dreadful diseases.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but I cannot see how his remarks are directly related to the Health League of Canada, which organization is getting a grant of $10,000. I think it is the wish of the committee at this time that all remarks should be strictly relevant to the vote under consideration.

Would the minister tell us what the Health League is for and why a sum of $10,000 is to be given to it? Apparently it is not attempting to do anything, because if it does not try to find the causes of
[The Chairman.]
and remedies for such things as arthritis, cancer and other serious ills, what is the use of having the league? Will the minister tell the committee what the Health League of Canada is, why this committee should be giving it $10,000, and why it should not be giving it $25,000 if it is worth supporting?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The Health League of Canada has been in existence for twentydive years. During that time it has carried on exceedingly valuable work-
In connection with what?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Will you please let me go on without interruption?
You interrupted me a few moments ago, stopped me from talking.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I did that in accordance with the rules of the house in order to raise a point of order which I thought it was my duty to do. The Health League of Canada is an educational organization. I do not think it does any research work; I have never heard of its doing any research and it is not part of its functions to do any research. When it was first established its work was largely concentrated on educational activities in connection with the reduction of venereal disease. That field of activity was broadened out subsequently, and it did a great deal of work in connection with immunization, particularly of children, so as to prevent their taking a number of diseases which could be prevented by that means. For example, in November of last year they put on a campaign from one end of Canada to the other which secured highly favourable results. It has also done special work in connection with industrial health, with nutrition and with securing the pasteurization of milk. It is in these five fields that the Health League of Canada has specially operated. Incidentally it may have done promotional or educational work in connection with cancer, but it is no part of its function to do any research. Grants to the Health League of Canada were commenced in 1919, when $5,000 was given. They have been carried through at various figures.
In addition to the money received from the federal government, the Health League of Canada receives grants from other bodies and from the general public as well. It has a wide influence in promoting interest in health. It has public meetings; it distributes its magazine, shows, films, distributes pamphlets, and at the request of local authorities directly carries on such campaigns as that to secure the introduction of laws requiring the pasteurization of

Supply-Health and Welfare
milk. Altogether it is a most useful organization, doing great work. As hon. members who are interested in health matters are well aware, it has always taken an active interest in the voluntary health committee of the Senate and the House of Commons It has been very useful indeed in helping the chairman and officers of that committee in securing desirable speakers for the various meetings of that committee which are held throughout the year. I support what the hon. member for Lethbridge said as to its being a desirable institution and I hope the committee will pass this vote.
Is the Health League of Canada carrying on a national campaign throughout Canada at the present time with respect to cancer?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No. I think the hon. member must have in mind the Canadian cancer society, which has been carrying on an effective campaign throughout Canada.

Has the Health
League of Canada anything to do with that organization, directly or indirectly?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No connection whatsoever. It is possible that the health league or some of its officers may have been helpful in the inauguration of the Canadian cancer society in 1938, and suggested its formation. But I do not think its activities with regard to cancer go any farther than that.

We must take it from what the minister has said that he desires no further discussion in the house this year on the matter of cancer. He does not want any discussion in any way whatsoever as to the seriousness of the disease, any discussion as to the possible means of finding a remedy, any discussion as to the activities his department should take in order to make sure that a remedy may be found, or that it would be publicized, introduced and applied throughout Canada when it is found. Do I take it from what the minister has said that from this time forward there is to be no more discussion in this session on the matter of cancer, under any heading?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
It is not for me to say what the house shall or shall not discuss. That is for the house to say, in accordance with its rules. Certainly the rules are clearly laid down, and the hion. member well knows that when we are in committee of supply only those matters pertinent to the item before the committee are to be discussed. The hon. member for Lethbridge must know that better than I do, because he has been here longer than I have. If there is an appropriate
time for the further discussion of cancer, I would welcome it. But with all respect I must say, and I think the hon. members who have been here during the discussion we have had on cancer will agree, that we have already had a very full discussion of cancer in connection with these estimates.

I believe that the Health League of Canada is deserving of the support of all parties in the house, and that the increase in this year's estimates will have the support of all. The league is doing outstanding work, a work which I believe is not equalled in any other country. I believe that at this time branches have been established in all the provinces.
Its great work has been in the field of adult education, and its success in securing the support of the daily and weekly newspapers in practically all cities across Canada is some indication of the value of its work. I believe, too, that it has received free advertising on Canadian street cars which could be valued at some tens of thousands of dollars. Its works in matters of nutrition and in public education based on good health seem to be sound, and have received the approval of the general public.
The committee has had ample opportunity to see some of its work. Through its efforts and those of the government we have had the privilege of hearing such men as Doctor Sigerist of Johns Hopkins university, Sir Wilson Jamieson from the British government and, more recently. Professor Tisdall of Toronto. The committee will welcome this increase in the vote, and we would hope that in the near future it might get back to the figure of $20,000, at which it stood some years ago. I should be remiss if I did not pay tribute to Doctor Gordon Bates, who has been in Ottawa frequently urging members to show an interest in this matter, because the league knows that the support of public men in Canada is most valuable to it in carrying on its educational work.

What is the membership of the Health League of Canada? How many branches has it, and where are they located? What is its annual income? How many of its officials are paid1, and what are their salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The latest statement in my possession shows an income of $78,811.51. I believe it has branches in several provinces.
One or more?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I believe it is organized on a basis of provincial branches. It has a small staff of paid full-time workers.

I asked two questions to which I did not receive answers. What is the membership of the league; what are the names of the -paid1 employees, and how much are they paid?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I have not the names nor salaries of the employees. The support of the Health League of Canada is to a large extent
IMr. Claxton.]
on the basis of affiliated organizations. A large number of organizations support it, receive its publications and the like. I have not a note as to the number of members, nor do I think there is any such record here. It is not an organization which charges a membership fee of a dollar or ten dollars. It is a voluntary organization primarily for educational purposes, and very largely supported by other institutions.

The committee would be interested to know the size of the league. We are asked to vote money for it, and' we should have some idea of how it is constituted and of what its membership consists. What is the total amount paid in salaries by the league?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have not that information, but I am sure that by using the long distance telephone I could secure that information before eight o'clock.

The other night Doctor Bates mentioned that a film was to be made in connection with the pasteurization of milk. Will some money be transferred from this vote, or will the cost be borne wholly by the film board?

speechtext: If a film on pasteurization is decided upon it would be financed by the Department of National Health and Welfare out of one of the votes for information. The film would then be shown by various means throughout Canada and one or more prints of it would be made available to the health league of Canada. The health league would also assist with technical advice in the preparation of the film. It is planned to have such a film at the present time.

If the health league of Canada considers that this vote is sufficient, I am happy to support it, but I think it is a small sum to vote to such a valuable organization. The results it has achieved, particularly in connection with publicity, have been remarkable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I agree emphatically with what the hon. member has said. I would point out that the work of this organization should not be measured by the size of this grant. While the grant is substantial in itself, it is perhaps more important in showing the interest of the federal government in the work, and it may be that this is useful as a spark plug in assisting the organization to secure a large part of the support it gets. For instance, in connection with its campaign on immunization it was able to secure many tens of thousands of dollars worth of free publicity because of donations made by national advertisers and others. It has an

active executive head in Doctor Gordon Bates, and I think we can look forward to its doing valuable promotional work in this field.

336. Canadian National Institute for the Blind, $18,000.
Is this the same amount as was voted last year for this institute?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes.
In view of the excellent work done by this institute is there any thought of increasing the grant?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: This same grant has been paid since 1931. The Canadian National Institute for the Blind, and the other institutes for the blind which are mentioned, have done exceedingly fine work, particularly in training the blind to look after themselves. This is only part of the money they receive, and the work they do must not be measured by the size of this grant.

I notice that the three other organizations which I assume carry on in the province of Quebec are receiving a total of $12,000, while only $18,000 is being given to the Canadian National Institute for the Blind which carries on work throughout the whole of Canada, including Quebec. Everybody knows about the excellent work it is doing and it is finding it a little hard to get sufficient money with which to carry on. Does the institute receive anything from the Department of Veterans Affairs for the work it does in connection with blind veterans?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I cannot answer that. I would point out that the income of the Canadian Institute for the Blind is considerable, being something close to $700,000.
It is more than that; it runs to between two and three million dollars because of its commercial work.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The last statement we have shows its total income for the year ended March 31, 1944, as $675,901.20.

That would be subscriptions and donations only, but the rest of its total income is from commercial work. It gets a couple of million dollars from that.
Mr. MacNI'COL: I believe the value of this vote is in the impetus it gives to a large number of men and women who are associated with the Canadian National Institute for the Blind across Canada to carry on its efficient and splendid work. I believe the head of
this institute, Lieutenant-Colonel Eddie Baker, was the founder. Lieutenant-Colonel Baker had the grievous misfortune of having his eyes drawn out by the suction of a shell that passed near his face during the first great war. Fortunately the shell did not hit him or he would have been killed. I believe he has been given some other title, an O.B.E. or something like that, and he is certainly worthy of any title this country can give him.
He has done marvellous work in connection with the national institute for the blind and the department is to be complimented upon supporting the work even to this extent. I presume if they had to have more the department would give them more. I agree with the hon. member for St. Paul's who states that many generous men and women throughout Canada are happy and willing to support this institute with time and means. We have all seen examples of their work. They have placed many blind men in booths in hospitals, city halls, public buildings and other places where they are able to make their own living. They have been given some purpose in life and it is interesting to note how happy they are. This wonderful work is worthy of support by the government.

I notice there are grants to four institutions for the blind and I presume the minister can explain why four grants are necessary. Can he tell us something of the welfare work being done by the different institutions? I know something about the work being done by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind but I know nothing about the other three. I always thought the Canadian National Institute for the Blind was all-inclusive, but apparently it is not and perhaps the minister could give ua a brief outline of the work done by the other organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Hon. members are familiar with the fine work done by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, and I think I should say a word about the other three organizations. L'Association Canadienne Fran-gaise des Aveugles is established in the province of Quebec, largely in Montreal. It carries on work corresponding to the work done by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. It assists the blind by giving instructions in the manufacture of fibre brooms, whisks, mops and all that kind of thing. Training is given in piano tuning, and employment is found in this kind of work. The association also provides the blind with free transportation and provides meals for blind
Supply-Health and Welfare

workers. It organizes social activities for the blind. The grant to this association was first made in 1927. _ It was carried on until cuts were made, as in all these grants, in 1932, and it has since been at the present figure. This association is also assisted by the province of Quebec, the city of Montreal, and Federated Charities.
The Inetitut Nazareth is an organization established in Montreal. It has to do primarily with hospitalization of the blind) and the education of the blind in music, classical studies, vocational training, and reading Braille. It supplies Braille books for the blind. Grants have been made to this organization from 1928 until they were reduced, in 1932. Since then, the grant has remained at the same figure. This organization also receives a grant from the province, the school commission, and the city of Montreal.
The third organization, the Montreal Association for the Blind, carries on in Montreal activities similar to those carried on by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. It has workshops where instruction is given in vocational training and in Braille. There is a school for the blind, particularly for blind boys and girls. It has a home teaching and social service department. This organization has received a grant from 1927 up to 1932, when like the others it was reduced. It also receives grants from the province of Quebec, the city of Montreal, and Catholic Charities.
I am in a general way familiar with the work of all these organizations, which are doing very good work. There is, I believe, no overlapping or competition between them, and the grants have been made to them, as I have said), for a number of years past.

I am pleased with the minister's explanation of the need for these grants. I think we are all satisfied with his explanation, and with his assurance that there is no overlapping because that is exceedingly important. Those of us Who do not live on the island of Montreal, when we see these three organizations centred in the island of Montreal, naturally hope that they are not getting special favours, and the. minister has given us that assurance.
A query enters my mind in connection with the Canadian grants to institutions for the blind. Does the department make compensatory grants in all provinces for educational purposes for the blind and, if so, under what vote might such items be found? People in the city of Montreal are favourably situated for receiving musical instruction and the other advantages mentioned by the minister. Do
	j
the blind in other parts of Canada receive equivalent training through institutes for the blind, that might be available to them? How are these particular grants reconciled with the needs of the blind in other parts of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My understanding is that the Canadian National Institute for the Blind does the job for all the rest of Canada. These three organizations in Montreal and the province of Quebec have gone on for some time, and two of them may have developed because of the difference in language. Of course, the majority of the people in the province of Quebec are French-speaking, and that may make a difference. I know that the Canadian National Institute for the Blind does give service in Quebec, but the same services are not, so far as I know, given to the same people who are served by other organizations.

I just wanted to point out the extra work that has been taken on by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind in caring for the blind casualties of the war. That is why I brought the matter up. They have a new hall in Toronto near where I live, Baker Hall, with room for fifteen or sixteen returned boys from overseas, but they have not room for the others whom they wish to take in and they have to make other arrangements. That costs money. The people of my city are very glad, of course, to subscribe. Many splendid subscriptions have come in from individuals, but it would encourage the organization if they were given a larger grant.

This institute, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, was the pioneer in Canada in doing this wonderful work. It is headed now by Lieutenant-Colonel Edward Baker, a much decorated soldier and patriot. He was a brilliant engineer, a graduate of Queen's university, who went to the first great war and lost his sight. He has also lost a very fine young son serving as a brave officer with the navy in the second world war. This institute for the blind is largely dependent upon subscriptions, tag days and that kind of thing. But the time has come when this country should do more for the blind. We who sit around this building, costing $22,000,000, will be blind if the lighting conditions are not improved soon because we cannot see here without artificial light. I am afraid the minister is a little blind as to what this institute is doing. It has had a hard, uphill fight, but the directors with the aid of a very fine newspaper have carried on this work right along, without the recognition it should have from the public or govern-

Supply-Health and Well are
ments. Many of the school children of our cities and towns have defective vision. The board of education in Toronto conducts special classes for those with defective vision, and the health department of our city has spent a vast sum of money for medical services and for care for those with defective vision and other complaints.
This matter of the blind is a national question affecting every country in the world. Blindness is the worst affliction that can happen to anybody, and all we are granting is a measly $18,000. A deputation going to New York over the week-end would spend that much. Every Tom, Dick and Harry, who wants to, can take a joy ride at the public expense nowadays. I am not objecting to trips. I have no time for any myself. We had a parsimonious controller, Controller Foster, afterwards mayor, in Toronto at one time. He was a member of this house for some time, and he used to call these trips "joy rides". They may not be altogether joy rides. Some of those going on these joy rides ride in chariots, others in planes, others in trains, none on foot. We. cannot afford to spend all the money we do on conventions and curtail necessary work such as for the blind with pin-money. In last night's Citizen there is a picture of the Minister of Health and Welfare going to a convention in New York, accompanied by a whole retinue of A.D.C.'s, and so on. I do not object to trips, but I think they have been overdone, especially when people want retrenchment. I wonder whether parliament has any conception of its obligations to the men, women and children of this country who are suffering from the disease of blindness, and the number of soldiers and soldiers' children who require help. It is a national problem. I am not opposed to large expenditures for this national health department. It should be one of the main departments of the * public service because, after all, what is life to anybody who has lost his health? This department should be expanded until it becomes the main department of the public service.
