Miscellaneous grantstil. Victorian Order of Nurses, $13,100.

Having had a great regard over the last few years for the splendid work which is being done by the Victorian Order
of Nurses, knowing what a magnificent work they are doing across Canada, I should like to draw to the attention of the minister one or two facts in connection with this organization.
First, I feel that the grant is altogether inadequate. It was instituted some ten years ago and has never been increased; at least I believe the grant was the same in 1934 as it is to-day; and the order has increased considerably since then, and deserves far greater support.
Let us for a moment consider the following facts. The number of Victorian Order branches is 101. Of these, twenty-seven have been organized during the last ten years since the grant was set up.
The number of patients served during 1945 was 100,118. The number of visits made during that year was 756,984; of these 50 per cent were free and 48 per cent were part paid.
Home nursing service is provided for patients on returning from hospitals, thus releasing hospital beds for more acutely ill patients.
The federal grant has been $13,100 per annum since 1934. The number of branches has increased by 36 per cent during the last ten years. Revenue has been considerably reduced by declining interest rates and more especially by depletion of capital funds to cover operating deficits. Expenses have increased sharply with expansion of service, and it has been necessary since 1934 to offer scholarships and uniform allowances in excess of $70,000 to attempt to maintain and build up a force of skilled public health nurses to ensure an efficient and adequate nursing service throughout Canada.
The Victorian Order of Nurses is financed by assistance from several sources, such as fees from patients, fees from insurance companies, government grants, public and private subscriptions and donations; and to give the committee some idea of the necessity of more funds to carry on this great service, the financial statement shows that in 1945 excess expenditure over revenue was $42,575.38. Just at this moment it is possible to carry on by making up this amount by using capital from endowments.
To save time, and with the unanimous consent of the committee, I have a financial statement which I should like to place on Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
When this item was before the committee before, I did endeavour to explain, to the best of my knowledge at the time, how it was arrived at. I might tell the committee that at that very moment the deputy minister of welfare was in Halifax meeting a number of representatives of welfare [DOT]organizations and some of the provincial
[The Chairman.]
officers and was actually discussing the organization of this work.
This vote is designed to cover payments not provided for in other votes for salaries but largely to be made to people outside the government services in connection with the investigation of cases where it has been reported to us, or where we have got knowledge, that the family allowance money is not being properly applied by a parent. Hon. members will appreciate that, with 1,420,233 families in receipt of family allowances, there is bound to be a number about which the information on file is not complete, so that a further investigation is required. There are also cases about which there has been a suggestion or a report that the money is not being applied for the welfare of the child. If we did not have a service to do this work I am sure hon. members would feel that we were neglectful of our duty. I think all hon. members see the necessity of having an item of this kind, and the one question really is, how much is needed for the purpose?
The basis on which the estimate was prepared-and I would recall again to hon. members the fact that estimates are prepared in November of each year-was this: the dependents' allowance board and the dependents' board of trustees were agencies of the federal government which had under administration large sums of money which were paid to dependents of members of our armed forces. At one time the figure was as high as 550,000 to 600,000 recipients. It was a large-scale operation, and there it was found necessary to investigate a considerable number of cases. The basis of payment for these investigations varied, but usually it was $3.50 for each report, plus seven cents a mile for travel necessitated in making the report. It was figured that the average cost of making reports was $5, and when the dependents' board of trustees came into existence it made a standard payment of $5 for each report. That figure was taken by the officers of the department and discussed with welfare workers and others who had expert knowledge; it was found to be a suitable figure, and in arriving at our estimates in making the arrangements which we have already made it was done on the basis of $5 a report.
The next question was, how many cases would we be likely to have? In discussions with those who had the most experience in this field, it was found that we might expect to have as many as three per cent of the total number of families about whom reports would be required each year on one ground or another. That figure was considered to be a good estimate. The dependents' allowance

Supply-Health and Welfare
board had in one year 38,000 referals, as they are called, or 7i per cent. We estimated, however, that it would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of 3 or 3^ per cent. On that basis we entered into an arrangement with Nova Scotia on the 1st of November under which the province undertook to make these investigations in consideration of a payment of $5 for each report, and it received a guarantee of 81,050.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: For what time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Per month. In Nova Scotia we are making payments to 76,473 families, and this payment of 81,050 a month represents about 3-3 per cent of the families there. On that basis we would require 8230,000 yearly for reports across Canada. The figure of 8300,000 was set down as including not only that 8230,000, but also payments that might [DOT]have to be made in connection with the administration of family allowance payments where there was no father, no mother, no children's aid society or anyone else responsible for the child. In such cases it has been found necessary to make some payment to an individual or to an agency for making a report and for handling the money, and on the basis of experience in this field it was considered that might amount to $50,000. The balance was considered as needed for administration.
When hon. members call attention to the fact, that our expenses during the year ended March 31, 1946, were only about $6,000 under this item, I would point out that these expenses were only made in respect of the province of Nova Scotia and only made for a period of four months. If you apply even that expenditure of $6,000 to Nova Scotia for the full year and then take that figure as the one which is proper for all Canada, you have to multiply the $6,000 by 50. In other words, the payment to Nova Scotia is for about one-third of the year, and it is in respect of something like one-twentieth of the population. So that, to apply the Nova Scotia payment to all of Canada for a full year we should multiply the expenditure for Nova Scotia by 50. This brings us the figure of $300,000 which we seek for this year.
Hon. members will appreciate that this is not an easy service to establish on a sound basis. We gave it careful consideration before making the agreement with Nova Scotia and did not proceed with agreements with other provinces, or undertake to set up services in other provinces, until we had gained more experience. On the basis of the experience we have, we have now made arrangements with Manitoba and British Columbia and are considering what should be done in the other
provinces. Our experience, I should tell the committee in all frankness, is that this figure of three per cent which we estimated might be the proportion of cases requiring investigation seems to us now, on the basis of our experience so far, a high estimate. It certainly will not be exceeded and we hope it will be very much reduced. I believe that the amount sought now in the estimate, in the light of this explanation, is justified in view of our lack of experience of anything that would warrant less. In other words, the figure is arrived at on the basis of past experience available. If our experience proves better than past experience, then we shall certainly not spend this sum and1 shall come back in another year and ask for less.

With all deference to the minister, the statement he has given us today has not, I suggest, contributed very much to the real information of the committee concerning the item. What the minister has said to-day has been largely a defence of the fact that he brought the item into the house in this large amount, and as to how it came about. The factors on which he has proceeded were taken into consideration seven or eight months ago, but that is not the situation with which we are dealing at the present time. It is not what was in the minds of the officials when they made up the item in November, 1945. The committee is going to consider the situation as we find it to-day. What is the situation? The fact of the matter is that, for the months of the last fiscal year during which this money was being used, a total' of $5,995 was expended. We had it from the minister on Monday last that in the first two months of this fiscal year a total of $5,000 was expended out of $300,000. But what advantage do we derive from the minister's multiplication exercise on the basis of this service being in operation in all provinces for twelve months of the year? That is not the situation that exists. The minister has sought to defend the miscalculation in the need in this respect by saying that he had an agreement with only one province in the fiscal year 1945-46. But at the present time the dominion has agreements with only three of the provinces, and they are not the largest provinces, at that. We are not told what type of investigation is planned by the dominion in respect of the provinces with which the dominion does not sign agreements. Are we to infer that this money is to be required only in the case of provinces with which the minister enters into agreements? If so, the case that the minister has made out is a case for a very small amount indeed.
May I say with all possible emphasis that the case made out to-day in substantiation of
Supply-Health and Welfare

an estimate of $300,000 is a case which, on examination, will not justify the expenditure of more than $25,000 or $50,000. We are not concerned with multiplication on the basis of a situation which does not exist; we are concerned with the situation as it exists to-day. Agreements have been made with three provinces. One-quarter of the fiscal year has passed. This investigation service has not been established in six other provinces. In the face of that the minister still asks the committee to approve the appropriation of $300,000. For my part I wish to protest against an appropriation being sought in that way.

May I get a little information from the minister on the matter just discussed by the hon. member for Eglinton. Is he right in assuming that the investigations referred to will be carried out only in provinces where there are agreements?
That is not so.
That is the whole basis of his argument.
No, it is not.

I am not quarrelling with the hon. member; I merely wish to get the record straight. The minister defends the estimate on the basis of the fact that the agreement will be extended to include all the provinces. That is what he said the other day. To-day the hon. member for Eglinton comes back and says that the appropriation is too large and that there is no agreement with six of the provinces. It is possible that there will be no agreement with Ontario and Quebec, particularly if they follow the attitude adopted at the dominion-provincial conference. As I understand it, the Family Allowances Act applies to all the children of Canada with one exception, and I shall argue that point with the minister at some future time. Whether there is an agreement with the provinces or not, I think the investigations set up by the government are necessary, and family allowances should be applicable to all provinces whether the premiers of those provinces like it or not. Am I right in assuming that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Certainly. I must say I can understand the attitude of the hon. member for Eglinton, but he says that the estimate is not dealing with the situation which exists to-day. The item is to cover, not the service we have to-day, but a system which is in full operation, and which we are aiming to put into full operation as soon as we can do it in a

sensible way. I must say that we are glad we did not go ahead and set up the kind of system we had in mind at one stage, which would have led to great expense, much more than $300,000. We were cautious about it and worked it out with one province. I think we gave them too high a guarantee. We do not expect to give any further guarantees.
But just take it as it is. The payment to Nova Scotia will be $12,600 per annum. Nova Scotia represents one-twentieth of the population of Canada, and we have to provide a service for all of Canada. In provinces other that Nova Scotia, Manitoba and British Columbia, we do these investigations now, in so far as they are necessary, through our own staff. But we believe that with changing conditions and the continued payment of family allowances, we ought to give a better service. We intend to give a service which will go right across Canada and which will, by one means or another, get precisely the same type of report in every part of Canada. In some provinces it will be done directly through the provincial agencies; but some provinces have not agencies of the kind which can do that work. In other provinces it will be more economical for us to make arrangements either with individual agencies directly or else even conceivably to employ personnel of the federal government. We want to do what is sensible and do the job with as little expenditure of money and as little trouble to the people as we can.
When the hon. member suggests that $25,000 or $30,000 would be enough-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes. I have to point out that we are spending $12,600 in Nova Scotia, a province having one-twentieth of the population of Canada. With all respect, I point out that the amount mentioned by the hon. member is not enough. If we can get this service established just as quickly as we can on the basis of our experience, then we are going to need a large sum of money. How much it is I do not think anyone can tell on the basis of experience to-day. But for a full year it will be $300,000, or something in that neighbourhood. How much less than $300,000 it will be for this year I just cannot say, because it depends on how quickly we can get the job done and how cheaply we can do it. Therefore I would ask the committee to pass this vote in the light of the explanation given. To set down a lesser sum than $300,000 would be misleading. I can assure

Supply-Health and Welfare
hon. members that we shall spend just as little as we can to do the job as speedily as we can.

The minister has made reference to the agreements with Nova Scotia, Manitoba and British Columbia, and said that they provided for an investigation service at an agreed fee per case. I do not think he has said that that was all that the agreements provided for.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I think that is all.
Do the agreements not go any farther than simply providing for an investigation service at a fee per case?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is right.

The next question has to do with efforts made to negotiate agreements with the other six provinces. Would the minister tell us briefly what negotiations have been undertaken in that respect, and what progress has been made?

If I might, I would make a further comment on something said this afternoon by the hon. member for Broadview. Ordinarily one would not take the time to comment on anything he might say with regard to representation at an international conference, or anything of that kind. However, in view of his remarks and the newspaper photograph he was showing, which I understood was a photograph of the Canadian delegation to the world health conference which is now being held at Hunter college in New York, I wish to say this. His references to joy rides or something of that kind might ordinarily be ignored, but on this particular occasion there were included in the Canadian delegation three distinguished doctors. I refer to Doctor Charles W. McMillan, president of the Canadian Public Health Association; Doctor T. C. Routley, executive secretary of the Canadian Medical Association, and Doctor Groulx, health officer of the city of Montreal. Everyone who knows anything about public health in Canada will recognize them as being outstanding in their fields.
These gentlemen consented to become part of the Canadian delegation. They went to New York without remuneration and arrived there before the conference began so as to become familiar with its work. They have put in long hours in loyal service to the people of Canada. I would not mention this except that I have worked with them and I feel that they might misconstrue what has been said by the hon. member for Broadview. I am sure the hon. member had no such intention. In referring to this department he stated his desire to see it become the major department in the service of the people of Canada, which I think indicates his intentions.
When conferences such as this are being held, at which representatives of Canada work with representatives of other nations to arrive at a basis of international cooperation, it is important that on technical subjects we should be able to secure the attendance of not only
representatives of the government and of the civil service of Canada but outstanding representatives of other fields of endeavour. It will not be easy for any government in Canada to secure that representation if remarks such as those that were made this afternoon are allowed to go uncontradicted.
These gentlemen are outstanding. They have worked long hours day by day through the heat of New York and they have done an outstanding job for Canada. We hope we shall be able to secure the services of equally distinguished people to assist Canada in making an effective presentation of her case at world conferences when it is our duty to attend such conferences. To serve Canada these gentlemen have sacrificed time that would have been spent on their own businesses or a well-earned holiday.
Attendance at one of these conferences is nothing in the nature of a "joy ride." Nor is it a joy ride to spend two or three days in New York and then try, during the remainder of the week, to do the work which would ordinarily be done in the whole week. It is no joy ride to work long hours with representatives of other countries, and it is no joy ride to spend yourself, as these gentlemen have been spending themselves, in the interests of their fellow Canadians and of mankind.

speechtext: The minister has not told us what steps are being taken by the department in the absence of agreements with the other six provinces with reference to investigations. I would ask him to tell us briefly of the plan he is following in provinces with whose governments there is no agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STATISTICS BASED ON FAMILY ALLOWANCES PAYMENTS
speechtext: I believe I said this afternoon, perhaps not sufficiently fully, that in each province we have a regional office which has to do with family allowance administration, and in those offices are a number of people who deal with these cases. In Prince Edward Island most of the. cases have been dealt with by Major Nicholson, the regional director. In the larger provinces welfare supervisors have been appointed and these investigations are made by permanent employees under their direction. We are assisted greatly by the voluntary work of representatives of children's aid societies, welfare organizations, churches, municipalities and other bodies. So far, this voluntary assistance has enabled us to do part of the job, but as we go along we shall either make arrangements with the provinces that have welfare organizations or engage our own staff to complete the picture so as to give service in every part of Canada.

maintopic: STATISTICS BASED ON FAMILY ALLOWANCES PAYMENTS
speechtext:
On May 31 when the estimates of this department were before us the hon
Supply-Health and Welfare

member for Yorkton brought to the minister's attention, what looked like a case of maldistribution in departmental personnel across the country. He pointed out that of 197 persons in one branch of the department there was only one stationed) in Saskatchewan, a province that is trying to take large forward steps in the field in which the minister is interested. We have in Saskatchewan one-half of one per cent of the staff doing this type of work throughout the dominion, for a population totalling seven per cent of the country as a whole. That does not suggest a fair distribution of the department's personnel.
I cannot find fault with the Minister's explanation to the hon. member for Yorkton, but his reply made me curious about the staff in Regina which handles family allowances. I happen to know a number of the persons employed in that branch and I can say that many of them have not had previous experience in national health and welfare work. I presume they have been selected for their administrative qualities.
The details of this item show an amount of only $63,270 for the permanent staff in the family allowances division, while $774,480 is being provided for temporary assistance and $225,000 for what is called casual labour. Is provision to be made in the future for a larger proportion of permanent employees? It seems to me that we have too much of the temporary and casual type of help in a large number of departments. The establishments are not sufficiently well organized that permanent employees can be appointed after examination by the civil service commission. Would the minister give the number of persons employed by his department at Regina, both permanent and temporary employees, together with any recent figures he has on the employment of casual labour?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STATISTICS BASED ON FAMILY ALLOWANCES PAYMENTS
speechtext:
The number of employees in the health branch of the department in Saskatchewan is four on a permanent basis and ten on a temporary basis, making a total of fourteen. In the welfare branch, all related to family allowance administration, there are thirty-eight temporaries, and the establishment of that regional office is forty-five.
As I have explained before, and as hon. members know, in a department which is just being set up the practice is to create almost all positions as temporary until it is found that they are really necessary to do the job. Then they are made permanent positions and permanent appointments are made to those posts. The reason why we have a considerable number of casual assistants was that in undertaking the work of registration and verification of families for the family allowance we had to deal right at the outset with all the children

in Canada under sixteen years of age, that is with sixteen years of children, whereas once the system gets going we have only to deal with the children bom each year. In other words, the administrative problem at first was one of dealing with something like sixteen times the normal load.

maintopic: STATISTICS BASED ON FAMILY ALLOWANCES PAYMENTS
speechtext: Did not the women's voluntary services assist considerably in that work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STATISTICS BASED ON FAMILY ALLOWANCES PAYMENTS
speechtext: Very much so. But as I was going on to say, in order not to create a permanent establishment very much larger than was necessary to do the job, we employed people in every regional office on a casual basis, as it is called. The hon. member for Regina City has referred to the great help given by various agencies, particularly women's voluntary services in the different capitals of the provinces of Canada during the time of registration, and I myself have already referred to that in previous discussions of this subject. We were very fortunate to secure in every province the assistance of large numbers of women volunteers to assist in the preliminary work of opening envelopes, sorting applications and doing the preliminary processing of them. The number of people who assisted in that way was several thousand. Had it not been for that assistance it would have been difficult indeed to begin payments as we did on July 18, 1945. Once the preliminary *work of processing applications was done, however, we did not look to voluntary assistance any further. But again I pay tribute to the great help we received in that way.

Gradually the staff has been worked into a pretty coherent whole and it is doing a good job.

administration of family allowances, included costs from three departments:	his own,

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STATISTICS BASED ON FAMILY ALLOWANCES PAYMENTS
speechtext:
With regard to the Department of National Revenue, that is not an expense against family allowance administration. There is, as the hon. member knows, a pay-back by some of the recipients of family allowances on account of the adjustment between income tax and family allowances, but there is no additional cost of family allowance administration there. With regard to the Department of Trade and Commerce, in respect of the vital statistics branch of the dominion bureau of statistics, all the items which relate to family allowances are paid for out of the family allowance vote. We make a payment to the dominion bureau of statistics for the services they render in this connection. With regard to Mines and Resources, in connection with family allowance payments to Indians and Eskimos, there is no additional payment. We have at Ottawa a regional office of family allowances dealing with family allowance payments for the northwest territories and the Yukon, and we there record the registrations, verify the births and issue the payments. It is of course possible that the burden on the Mines and Resources staff has been increased by reason of the fact that they have to help in the administration of family allowances payable to Indians and Eskimos in the northwest territories and the Yukon and also in other parts of Canada. They have assigned one of their officers to act as liaison officer in this connection, but he was previously an employee of the department. Consequently there is no additional expense in Mines and Resources, identifiable as such, though possibly it could be worked out that some part of the overhead of the department might be applicable to this extra work.

speechtext:
Has any thought been given to compensating the private welfare agencies for the additional work which has been cast upon them in the course of administering family allowances? I am thinking in particular of children's aid societies. Undoubtedly in the administration of family allowances through these societies there has been a great deal of extra expense incurred by them, and it would be only fair that they should receive some compensation for their extra work.
I have before me an extract from the report of the Children's Aid Society of the city of Toronto for the year ended September 30, 1945. Mr. Mills, the general superintendent, after speaking approvingly of the recent increase of 14 a month in the rate for the foster homes made possible by the family allowances, said in his report to the annual meeting that, "other than this, the family allowances have brought little, if any, relief to our funds, as they are deposited in a trust fund for each child, expenditures from which are required for additional benefits. The bookkeeping and other services in connection with the allowances are colossal and especially embarrassing at a time of acute shortage of both clerical help and office staff." May I ask the minister if any thought has been given to trying to assist in easing the burden of cost on these welfare organizations?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I should like to say that the department and the family allowance administration have the closest and most cordial relations with all welfare agencies throughout Canada, and particularly the children's aid societies, and I should like to link with them the name of Mr. Robert Mills, who has been particularly cooperative. The question the hon. member raises is one which has been put to us by the children's aid societies, and it has received a great deal of consideration and has been the subject of discussion with them. We think that, w'hereas it is pretty clear that the administrative costs of the societies have gone up owing to their being so useful in connection with family allowance administration, on the other hand the charges on the funds of the societies must have been relieved directly or indirectly, by an offsetting amount. This, I may assure the hon. member, is receiving consideration and will continue to do so. It would be difficult to work out a scale of payments, and our view so far is that what has been added to administrative expenses has been more than offset by the benefits to the wards of the children's aid societies themselves.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.

The federal government, by agreement, is paying Nova Scotia $5 for each report submitted by whoever is making the investigation, and if that is true and children's aid societies are used in the communities to carry out investigations, and there is not much travel involved, I think $5 per report is of considerable assistance to the organization. Personally, I think that, while these voluntary organizations may be doing some useful service, that kind of thing is not satisfactory. If the federal government under-
Supply-Health and Welfare

takes to pass a statute laying down certain regulations it should be responsible for the administration of the machinery and should have adequate staffs in each province to carry out the work. I do not think that any voluntary organization, no matter how honest or sincere it may be, has either the time or the facilities to do the kind of job that should be done. I recognize that the department started this thing and has made very good progress, and it is necessary to use various agencies because of shortage of man-power and woman-power. But in the final analysis, this being a permanent act, it will have to be administered by permanent officials. To have this work done by people who are on the job eight or nine hours a day doing their own work and who then try to carry on with other work in the evening or on an afternoon when they happen to be off duty is a method that does not make for efficiency. I should like to have the minister outline the mechanics in Nova Scotia, from the head office into the community, explaining how he gets the report back and exactly what part the children's aid society plays in the administration of the act in the province.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. The set-up w'ith regard to the family allowance administration in Nova Scotia is this. Family allowances come under the director of family allowances, who is located in Ottawa, and there are nine provincial offices. In Nova Scotia, as in the other provinces, the provincial office is located in the capital of the province. When the family allowance office there receives an application for registration which may not give satisfactory information and this cannot be obtained by correspondence, which is the ordinary method used first, or if a report is received from one source or another indicating that someone is not applying the money for the benefit of the child, then in either event, the family allowance administration, under the arrangement worked out with the province of Nova Scotia, sends a request for a report on the matter. That is sent to the welfare department of Nova Scotia. That department then gets a report either through its own employees or through the children's aid society, if there is one in the locality. Not all the territory of Nova Scotia is covered by children's aid societies.
The hon. member suggested that we should have our own officers in every part of Canada to do this job. There is a lot to be said for that; but had we started to do it in that way and had set up that scheme back in July, 1945, we would have found it exceedingly difficult to get adequate staff and there would
[Mr. Gillis.l
have been a great tendency to have at least one inspector for each electoral division across Canada. That would have been an easy way to deal with the matter administratively. It is followed in the case of the census and other things and that would have been the natural pattern. Moreover, that kind of set-up would not have been out of line with our own preliminary estimates of the need. Had we done that, I feel that, so far as we can see the need now, we would have spent a lot of money that we did not need to spend. We are still looking at the whole problem-that is what the hon. member wants us to do-and as I explained earlier to-day we hope to have an adequate service for every part of Canada worked out in the best possible way for that particular part and at the lowest possible cost to the people of Canada.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I do not want the minister to think I am critical of what has been done in Nova Scotia. He has there one of the most efficient set-ups in the dominion. They have done a marvellous job in the short time they have functioned. I have not received a complaint in any form, and I have had much to do with the Halifax office. It is, in my opinion, one of the most efficient offices the government has set up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: My point, however, is that I am a stickler for permanent officials where there is a permanent act to be administered. Under those conditions I do not believe in voluntary effort.

In the United Kingdom. That, of course, is on a contributory basis. It is included in the total social insurance contribution which is paid by practically the whole population.
In Australia they have a means-test plan under which pensions are payable to males at age sixty-five and to females at age sixty. The pension is 32s. 6d. per week, or $5.77 at the current rates of exchange. It is payable out of the welfare fund to which there is a substantial contribution paid by individuals. It is 7% per cent on incomes of most individuals and it is payable in respect of incomes over $360.
In New Zealand there is a dual system; one payable without a means test to males and females at the age of sixty-five, and a means-test plan payable to males and females at the age of sixty. It is going to take some
time to put both plans into effect. There again, it is payable out of a social security fund, to which individuals pay 7% per cent on their total incomes from the first dollar.
In the United States there is a plan of survivors' insurance, payable without means test to men and women at the age of sixty-five. The amount payable is related to the average wage. About three-fifths of the gainfully employed people are covered and the employers and employees each contribute one per cent on the first $3,000 of wages.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
Much the biggest item in the items referred to by the hon. member for Eglinton is the item covered by vote 572, old age pensions and pensions to the blind. This was introduced by order in council passed under the War Measures Act in 1942 and was designed to provide, in respect of old age pensions, something corresponding to the cost of iiving bonus. As I announced earlier this week, it is the intention of the government to bring in legislation at this session to put that change in the Old Age Pensions Act on a permanent basis.
The next item is for the treatment of' Canadian fishermen and seamen. That is to provide for payments for the cost of treatment required by persons employed on ships of Canadian registiy and seamen of Canadian citizenship sailing on vessels of any of the allied nations. That has been carried on, and it will not be continued beyond the period of reconversion.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: What does the minister construe as the period of reconversion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
Treatment may be claimed within a period of twelve months after the end of the war, and for injuries or illnesses originating prior to January 1, 1946.
Item 574 is a similar item. It is to provide treatment for non-resident merchant seamen while awaiting deportation, such deportation being impossible for the time being owing to shipping conditions, or to conditions in their countries of origin. So that, too, will totally disappear within the same period. It is decreased S10.000 from last year.
Item 575 is to provide a health unit at Prince Rupert, British Columbia. This is an amount of S4,080 furnished to the city of Prince Rupert to pay the salary of a medical officer whom the armed forces found it desirable to have at that point during the war. The amount of $2,040 will, we anticipate, be sufficient to cover the fiscal year, and there will be no continuation after that.
Item 576 covers health services in Halifax. This is an annual amount to assist the city of Halifax in maintaining and improving health conditions. Hon. members are aware of the fact that Halifax had an enormous
[Mr. Fleming. 1
increase in population, not only members of the armed forces, but also merchant seamen during the war. It was found essential to improve health services in connection with sanitation and so on durmg the war. This was a place where the increase in demand was peculiarly brought about by war conditions. Consequently this payment was provided for. It is a decrease from the amount which was previously paid. In 1945-46 the amount was 866,743.72, and it will stop this year.
Items 577 and 578 relate to payments for the chloramination of water systems at these points on the Pacific coast. During the years 1942-43 it was found necessary, to meet the requirements of our own armed forces and those of our allies, and the naval and merchant shipping, to instal chloramination systems in these localities. The cost of installation was borne by the federal government. The cost of operating the installation was also borne by the federal government. We have .now worked out with all the localities arrangements under which the federal government will not carry on the cost in any event after the end of the present fiscal year.
In three cases the localities are acquiring chloramination plants from War Assets Corporation on terms which seem to be fair, and our obligations in this respect will totally end at the end of the calendar year.
Item 579 deals with the treatment of repatriated merchant seamen. This is an amount of $5,000 to provide treatment for those repatriated merchant seamen who have been prisoners of war, and not otherwise entitled to treatment. There was a provision, as hon. members know, for the treatment of deep-sea sailors and interprovincial sailors, under the Canada Shipping Act. This provides similar treatment for those sailors who were unfortunate enough to be taken prisoners of war. It will certainly terminate at the end of this year.
The final item in this category is No. 580, for the women's voluntary services. This is an amount of $7,000. During the war the Department of National War Services had a women's voluntary services division which'did good work in organizing women across Canada to perform voluntary services. That division was transferred to the Department of National Health and Welfare not long ago. We anticipate that its work will not be continued by the department. We regard it as peculiarly a wartime activity, and our thought is that the functions which were hitherto carried on by that branch might more properly be carried on by voluntary organizations. This item of $7,000 is put in to cover the expenditure necessary on this division, pending its probable liquidation.

Altogether, items 572 to 580 amount to a total of $137,080, apart from the old age pensions provision. We anticipate that no part of these expenditures will be carried on after the end of the present fiscal year. These are definitely expenditures on demobilization and reconversion.

speechtext: When the minister answered my question a moment ago I believe he tied in his answer with the fact that he did not propose to go any farther with dominion-provincial agreements because the dominion-provincial conference had been adjourned. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
It must be within the knowledge of everyone who has studied old age pensions-and most hon. members have- that old age pensions are paid either on a means-test basis or as of right. The proposals made to the provinces provided for a payment of $30 a month to everyone at the age of seventy as of right, and payments of half the cost of pensions up to $30 a month in respect to people between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine based on a means test.
I think I am right in saying that in every countiy where a pension is payable as of right it is paid by virtue of contributions made by the individual, either in the form of a social security tax such as that of 7J per cent as is imposed in Australia and New Zealand, or in the form of payments out of wages as is the case in the United Kingdom, or in the form of a one per cent payroll deduction paid by the employer and employee as is the case in the United States. Our old age pension proposal was part of a comprehensive set of proposals, and it will be found that the proposals made to the provinces in August, 1945, contemplated a contributory old age pension scheme.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: What amount was it anticipated' would be paid by the individual?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: That was never definitely arrived at. It was discussed, and the kind of discussion was-I hope I am not revealing confidences, but this has been spread around a good deal-that there should be a social security tax of something in the neighbourhood of three or four or even five per cent.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: On income?	.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Yes. We have given every possible consideration to this question of old age pensions, and I must say I do not see how the federal government can pay old age pensions which will be contributed to by the people except on a nation-wide basis. It is difficult to see how it could be done without either a constitutional amendment or by agreement with the provinces. I am not expressing any final opinion on that, but that is the view we have after the consideration we have given to it. If that is so, and I believe it is so, I do not see how we can have a system of old age pensions such as the hon. member seems to have in mind except on the basis that all the pensions are paid out of consolidated revenue. If the hon. member wants to propose that as the attitude of his party, it is an interesting point of view, but I do not think he does.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I am only seeking information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance in his budget speech last night referred to this as one of the social security measures which the federal government had as part of its pro-gamme, but we cannot work it out in the existing situation. We hope to work it out just as soon as it is possible to do so.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Have the provinces been approached to see whether they would agree to this tax of three or four or five per cent as the case may be? What is to prevent the minister from going to the provinces and asking them if they are opposed to this social security tax being imposed? It does not enter into the general taxation agreement picture at all so far as I can see.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
Perhaps I should have said a word on that in answer to the hon. member for Trinity. In our view these things cannot be separated. If you are to have a budget which provides for $150,000,000 for health insurance, $200,000,000 for old age pensions of $30 a month at the age of seventy for everyone, a 50 per cent contribution by the federal government to the cost of old age pensions between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine for those needing it, at a minimum cost of $17,000,000, plus the dominion assumption of unemployment assistance at a rate of 85 per cent of the amount payable under the unemployment insurance provisions now in force, plus health grants which may run from $13,000,000 to $19,000,000, all in addition to the family allowance and the present unemployment insurance provisions, and on top of all that the provisions regarding public investment contained in the dominion government proposals, then I say you have a programme

Supply-Health and Welfare
which can be made to work and which is workable and comprehensive. But there is no way that I know of, of assuming responsibility for carrying out that programme unless the rest of the dominion government proposals are substantially agreed to. Any government should hive the power to discharge its responsibilities.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: You have power to impose this tax now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Yes, I will correct what I said. There is no restriction on the legislative jurisdiction of the federal government with regard to taxation, but there is, I think, a real desire on the part of the people of Canada to see that the dominion and the provinces work together so that these things may be worked out through cooperation and agreement, as we had hoped and still hope they will be, rather than in any other way.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: It is interesting to hear the minister talk all around the question and give some kind of analysis of last night's budget. But the fact remains that the social security measures of the dominion, which he says cannot now be undertaken, are to be paid for by a tax of three or four or five per cent on all incomes. There was no kick from the provinces over putting unemployment insurance into force. That is something that carries itself, and the dominion government went to the provinces and got permission to institute unemployment insurance. Is there anything to prevent the minister or the government from going to the provinces at this time and asking them whether they would like to have these social security measures put into force? The minister just skated around the whole question. Just because the dominion government cannot get its whole social security programme through now, it is going to deprive the people of Canada of what could go into force at the present time. There is no use in the minister talking like that. It just does not make sense. The dominion government has power now to impose this tax of three or four or five per cent and put these social security measures into force. So that it has no excuse for not going on with these measures if they are considered advisable. If the government considers them advisable, why not go ahead with them and get permission from the provinces to do so, get the consent of the provinces. I do not think they will kick about it. But certainly that has nothing to do with the general framework of taxation in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
I should like to traverse the hon. member's remarks as flatly and directly as I possibly can. Any item which requires the expenditure of 8200,000,000 a year 63260-1911
has a good deal to do with the general economic structure of this country. I shall not try to add anything to what has been said before, what was said by the Minister of Finance last night and what is contained in the dominion government proposals.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: The discussion has been most interesting. The fact remains that the dominion government made the largest social security commitments that ever were made in this country without ever consulting anyone. If they are prepared to go to the provinces now, they are going after the commitments have already been made, and asking the provinces to agree to something which the government have already done.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: If the hon. member and the committee will look at the text of the dominion government proposals, at the speeches from the throne in which they were first anticipated in January, 1944, and referred to in January, 1945, at the speeches of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and myself, I venture to say that they will find no place where it was not clearly stated that this was a comprehensive plan and that the dominion government was prepared to go forward with it, upon our working out the arrangements with the provinces. You will find that stated again and again in the documents to which I have referred. That was made perfectly plain.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Are you going to say you consulted the provinces before you introduced family allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: There was no need for us to consult the provinces before introducing family allowances.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: That is a large measure to *which you committed yourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
But if we had had family allowances on a contributory basis I do not see how we could have done it without consulting the provinces or securing an amendment of the constitution. That is the fundamental difference between the position with regard to what we did for family allowances and what was proposed to be done regarding old age pensions provided that we got an agreement with the provinces.
What was the purpose of the conference in August, 1945? It was to consult the provinces. Did we have to consult the provinces before we put forward a proposal? What we got them together for was to consult them, and we had that consultation at the conferences from August, 1945, on. I do not think hon. members would wish any government to
Supply-Health and Welfare

say to another government, "Before we even discuss a thing with you, have we your permission to discuss it?"

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: But you did it on unemployment insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: We did exactly what we did here; that is, we called them in to consult them. That is what we did in regard to old age pensions, health insurance and the whole of the dominion proposals. The purpose of the conference was to consult them, and we had that consultation.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: The question we originally asked with regard to old age pensions was, is the minister seeking any arrangement or agreement with the provinces separately with regard to old age pensions? I still cannot see why he cannot seek a separate agreement with them, or call a conference of the health ministers with regard to this subject and have them go back and ask their governments whether they are in favour of having such a social security tax as he spoke of earlier in his remarks. Just in case I may be misunderstood, I should like to put myself on record as being heartily in favour of old age pensions on a much, more liberal scale than .830 a month.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I have been very much interested in the comments of the Progressive [DOT]Conservative party, particularly having in .mind the comments made by their financial *critic last night following the presentation of the budget by the Minister of Finance. He emphasized again and again that now is the time to economize.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: What about false economy?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Are you for or against old age pensions?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I made my position quite clear, that I am in favour of them.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Then why attack us?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: The Conservative party stubbornly opposed the introduction of old age pensions in the first place.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: You are just talking through your hat. I was here in 1930 and was one of the supporters and advocates of the whole business.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
Do not try to lift yourselves on our shoulders. Go after the government yourself.
Mr. SKEY": Are you in opposition here, or are you for the government?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I am just drawing attention to the fact that we are hearing a great deal said about old age pensions by people who did very little about the matter when they were in a position to do so.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Your party will never be put in that position.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I should like to say to the minister that I think nearly 200,000 old age pensioners in Canada will be disappointed with the speech of the Minister of Finance last night-

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Now you are saying something.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: -and the minister's statement to-night. I cannot think that even though it did take $200 million a year to provide $30 for all the old age pensioners in Canada, as was suggested in the dominion proposals to the provinces, that should stop the government of Canada from making this gesture to the people in those brackets. When the family allowance proposal was brought down the expenditure was larger than this, and there have been very few criticisms across the country about that expenditure. Taking into account Canada's contribution during the war, when one considers that more than a million of our young people were in the services, that we gave away over four billion dollars worth of our materials in the form of mutual aid, and that we enjoyed a higher standard of living than ever before in the histoiy of Canada, I think it is unfortunate that the minister is not in a position to say to-night that something more definite will be done this year for the old age pensioners of the country.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
The city of Toronto had old age pensions twenty or thirty years before there was ever a C.C.F. party. It paid $12 a week, when it could get no federal or provincial aid, to those who were unable to work, and in addition it maintained a contributory system in the fire department, the police department, the school board and other departments. The principle of this old age pension and health legislation is that we are to consult the provinces. People are dying every' day while the government are consulting the provinces about health and old age pensions, and nothing can stop it, because the undertaker is there while all these consultations are going on.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Sooner or later we as a parliament must do something for these people, and at the same time have some check on departmental expenditures. Departments are spending money like water; yet we see no improvement in public health; the old age pensioners are not getting fair treatment, and they are subject to a means test which is the meanest thing ever created in the history of the country.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
I thought it would not be very long before the chickens of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario would be coming home to roost. I do not know when the Conservatives will learn to stop talking about "economy" in an age when we want anything but economy as far as expenditures on public services are concerned. I am not criticizing the Conservative members particularly, except that I do hope that they will begin to see the light after a while. I do not believe there is one item which has been presented in this house which the Conservatives have not been as eager to extend to those concerned as have the members of the C.C.F., the Social Credit, or the Liberal party. They have been eager to have better prices for farm commodities, better wages and all that sort of thing. To get up after that and talk about the need for economy is so grossly inconsistent that they make themselves ridiculous. The colleagues of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario should really take him off into his room some time and give him a fatherly talking to.
What I rose to say was this. It must be obvious to the members of the committee that the minister has succeeded pretty well in talking himself into a state of helplessness. In effect he says, here are these provinces; if they would only come and cooperate with the dominion we would be able to pay all these things we want to pay, but they won't. So this big powerful Canada with its wonderful resources, and this great big Ottawa government here, with all the power in the dominion-

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: And the big stick.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
-just can't pay. Well, that is one of the most foolish attitudes which can be taken, and one of the most impotent! I believe the day will come when the minister himself will laugh at the stand he is taking to-night.
May I just propound a simple question for the members of the committee to contemplate? Even if the provinces came to Ottawa and abjectly accepted every single proposal the dominion government offers, would the dominion then be able to offer old age pensioners in Canada 860 a month?- I think the minister would say, "No; we cannot do that."
Well, would they be able to offer that $60 a month at the age of fifty-five? I presume the minister would again say no. Or would they be able to give the blind anything like the pension they ought to have? Again the answer would be a pathetic no. Is that not enough to show that the whole method of approach of the dominion government is wrong? It is wrong because obviously the amount we can give to our elderly citizens depends on the goods we can produce, not the taxes we can collect, and in 1945 we were producing ten billion dollars' worth of goods. If we undertook to distribute that amount of goods so that the people could use them, $50 a month to people of sixty-five years of age would be no more than small change. Let us contemplate that seriously and then set about some modern way of learning how to distribute those goods. We must do it.
I want to lay down three or four points for the minister to consider, if the committee will bear with me.
The minister must not give up his old age pension proposals, nor must he give up his proposals in connection with pensions to the blind, simply because the provinces saw fit not to cooperate in the gigantic scheme of centralization of power which the dominion contemplated and endeavoured to bring into existence at the various conferences with the provinces.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Certainly; any question at all.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I am wondering how he arrives at the age of fifty-five. Why not fifty?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I will answer the hon. gentleman's question. Ultimately the age at which the old age pension must be paid is going to depend on the age at which industry is going to have no use any longer for the individual; in other words, the age at which he is going to be put out of his job.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Why not fifty?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
The age will probably have to be fifty. If I were to say fifty now, however, I have no doubt that 50 per cent of the Liberals would go on a campaign and get up on platforms throughout the country in an endeavour to make my remarks look ridiculous. Therefore, until the Liberals become a little more advanced in their ideas, I have to be somewhat reserved in what I say. Obviously the day will come when a man who has reached the age of fifty-that day has already come for the woman who has reached the age of fifty-will not be in any pre-
Supply-Health and Welfare

ferred position when it comes to obtaining employment in any concern in the country. Obviously, therefore, if we are to deal with the old age situation, we must be prepared to give the individual enough to enable him to live a life of dignity just as soon as the society in which he lives has no longer any need for his services. That, I think, is selfevident.
With that as the fundamental principle on which to work, let us go forward realistically, facing the facts. I maintain that the scheme which the dominion offered the provinces simply would not cope with the situation at all. They seek to bind the provinces hopelessly to a system of centralization and regimentation; and, notwithstanding that, they would not be able to deal at all effectively with the problems confronting the country. That being so, let us see if we cannot find another approach that will at least give some prospect of holding possibilities. The minister, I repeat, must not abandon his ideas with regard to old age pensions and pensions for the blind. He knows the kind of thing he would like to do. He is as forward-looking a man as there is in this house and just as desirous of seeing that things are done well in this country, and just as sympathetic and tenderhearted, just as considerate of humanitarian ideas as anyone else. Surely, then, he can go forward with his ideals, the ideals which his heart dictates, and see whether he can attain them without the kind of measures he has been thus far contemplating.
First of all, I would suggest, the contributory system for old age pensions is false. It is unsound. Just as soon as the productive agencies within the country catch up, there will be a surplus of every kind of goods and services. That is number one. The thing which we shall need in this country above all others will be purchasing power among the people, and how can you distribute purchasing power among the people if you take some away from every cheque they get in order to build up a fund with which to pay old age pensions? As soon as any Progressive Conservative or any other progressive in the house gets the answer to that question I invite him to call me up and tell me.
I say, therefore, that the contributory system is out in any genuinely progressive, streamlined, modern system of dealing with our situation.
What must we say next? The taxing system will be out. When we tax people in the way we tax them now we take from them the very purchasing power which they need in order to live, and which the producers of goods need

to have the people receive if they, the producers, are to sell their goods to the recipients of purchasing power. In other words, by our taxing system we are destroying the home market and destroying the distribution system. Clearly, then that method of approach is unsound, and that is the next fundamental principle to lay down.
May I say to the minister and to the members of this committee that there is no need of any change in the constitution of Canada. All these ideals we entertain with respect to old age pensions and pensions for the blind as well as other social services can be attained without in any respect destroying the constitution of the country.
May I say, in addition to that, that there is no need for centralization. Already several progressive ministers have begun to see that centralization is unsound. The Minister of Labour, on several occasions in the house this session, has pointed out that fact. Then why consider any scheme of centralization such as the dominion proposed at the conferences? Centralization is simply out. It must not be contemplated. I honour the provinces that have insisted that it shall not be brought about. If Premier Drew had done less than he did he would have betrayed his trust in these times. There may be ulterior motives in Premier Drew

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I am trying to be fair; I am not saying that there are; nor am I saying that there are any ulterior motives so far as Premier Duplessis is concerned. I take the conduct of these two gentlemen at its face value and I say that they have merited the honour of this dominion for the stand they took against centralization. It is a good thing that they did take that stand, because they are the premiers of two provinces which are so big that they cannot be taken into the woodshed and spanked. It is their responsibility to stand up and look after their weaker fellow provinces.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: What item is this?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
The item under which the minister was discussing the dominion-provincial conference. I, too, am discussing the dominion-provincial conference. Surely the hon. member for Saskatoon city is keen enough to see that; I do not need to give him a talking to. We listened for fifteen minutes to a talk clearly intended to indoctrinate into the members of the house and into the people of the country the idea of centralization. I am answering that argument. As I said a few moments ago, there will soon be a surplus of

Supply-Health and Welfare
goods and services in this country, a surplus with which we shall not know what to do. Already we are contemplating going out and seizing markets in South America and in other places.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Order. We are discussing old age pensions and pensions for the blind.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: That is exactly what I am discussing, Mr. Chairman. Just as soon as there is a surplus of goods and services in this country-[DOT]

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Order. The question of marketing goods and all that sort of thing has nothing to do with this item.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
I have left that
matter, Mr. Chairman. May I suggest that while we were discussing old age pensions it was not in order to spend a lot of time on the dominion-provincial conference any more than it is out of order for me to talk about what I am talking about. What I am talking about has a definite bearing on old age pensions. I was going to say that as soon as a surplus arrives there will be a tendency for wages to fall and for the price of goods to fall; there will be a tendency to go into a depression, and just as soon as that time comes, then will come the time for the creation of debt-free money in this country to represent that surplus of goods and services.
I warn the members of the committee that if they do not come to realize the soundness of what I am saying they are going to head this country straight into disaster. If the minister and his colleagues do not base their policies on the fundamental principle of debt-free money they will be responsible for leading this country into disaster, and we shall not have to wait many years to see the fruits of their good labours in that regard. That is important to bear in mind. Normally the production of the state, even before the war, increased year by year three, four and five per cent. When production increases in the state the amount of money in the state has to increase. Who is to supply that increase of money? I maintain that money must be supplied by the state with debt-free money and not by banks which lend money. Just as soon as the state begins to create debt-free money as tickets to represent the surplus goods and services which are in the country, that state will have found a new source of income, a new source of revenue with which can be paid the old age pensions and the pensions for the blind without additional taxation, without centralizing power, without modifying the British North America Act, for this Ottawa
government has control over the banking and financial system of this country, and it has the power to create an issue of debt-free money just exactly as the treasury board did create twenty-six millions of debt-free money during world war I, and use it. This can be done.
The	ACTING	CHAIRMAN	(Mr.	Golding) : Order.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
And it is the solution of the problem.

speechtext:
I am sorry; I could not hear what you said.

support the Chair and endeavour to stick to the rules.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
Where the difficulty lies is, as you, sir, must see, that the members of the committee have talked themselves into a state of impotency, of absolute ineptness. Until I started to speak there was not a suggestion as to what could be done from either the C.C.F., the Liberals or the Conservatives. Certainly the time had come for something progressive to be enunciated before them, and that is all I am doing. I am talking about how old age pensions can be paid without all the ruinous proposals which the minister has been contemplating all during the time that he has been defending himself before this committee.
I emphasize that point. When that is done we shall be going into a new order of debt-free money created by the state to represent the surplus goods and services which the state is able to produce as a result of the tremendous mechanization and the marvellous knowledge and technological skill which have come into this generation's possession.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: The printing press.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
The minister talks about the printing press! Why not? All the money the minister has in his pocket came out of the printing press. There is not a dollar of currency that ever came out of a bank in Canada that did not come out of the printing press. What is the matter with the minister? Why does he make a remark like that? He is moreover, entirely overlooking the fact that at least 97 per cent of the business of this country is done with bank credit. Why does not he recognize the fact-and in fact it is
Supply-Health and Welfare

more than a fact-that bank credit can be used as the new money that is debt-free and interest-free just as well as the printed money?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I could get up and make a propaganda speech on all these things and I could make a good job of it too.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: We have been dealing with old age pensions. We shall soon be in the position where we shall have to consult the provinces to play "the wearin' of the green" on the bagpipes. v

speechtext: Were not the provinces originally independent? They were independent when they entered confederation. What is the matter with the hon. member for Broadview?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I was going to ask the minister a simple question, but I think I shall now have to make a speech. I was sorry to hear the fallacious arguments of the hon. member for Mackenzie, who said that because we spent several billion dollars in the war we could now spend several billions more on various schemes of social security, and there should be nothing to it. It reminds me of the story of a man who had SI,800 in the bank and who was suddenly stricken with the terrible disease of cancer. He had an expensive operation which cost him $1,500. When he got out of the hospital he said. "I could afford to spend $1,500 to get rid of that desperate disease which I had and which I did not want, and I certainly ought to be able to afford to buy a new automobile, a new washing machine for my wife, refurnish the house and spend $3,000 or $4,000 more on other things without any trouble at all." I think that is what that argument amounts to.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Which argument?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I was referring to the hon. member for Mackenzie. So far as the hon. member for Lethbridge is concerned it has always been a marvel to me how he and the members of his party can come out with so many exceptionally sound statements which I can follow and agree with and at the same time advocate policies which in their essentials come down to the point of supporting old age pensions where the baby bonuses stop.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Tell us how you would do it?

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: It might be quite possible to do it; but having spent several years of close association with the founder of the Social Credit party in Alberta, and having had many hours of conversation with him while he was directing the group-
