maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: I am sorry; I was just replying to the question. I am sorry to say that after all that discussion and argument he was pleasant; but I was still absolutely unconvinced of the soundness of his ideas.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: Can you see a solution of the problem? That is what we want.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
To come more particularly to the old age pension matter, may I say that during the present session of parliament I have received somewhere in the neighbourhood of twelve to fifteen hundred cards from old people who wish to receive a higher old age pension. These cards are put out by an organization called the social security council of Alberta, which advocates $60 a month as the first principle for men at the age of sixty and for women at the age of fifty-five. The first card that was put out had the amount and urged the member to whom it was sent to carry that policy into effect. Then they put out a new card which threatens the member that if he does not put forth his best efforts, if he does not get this thing into operation, he will be defeated at the next election; they will make sure of that. I object to putting over some particular idea by making use of a cheap card through the mail, particularly when it comes without a stamp on it, and the government gets no revenue from it. I object to being threatened by these people.
But one point I should like to make is this, that so long as the old age pension situation remains in anything like its present state, there will be constant demands to increase the amount of that pension and to lower the age. That will go on and on and on; there will be constant demand and constant pressure.
As a result of having had all these cards, I have given considerable thought to the problem. In my view the only permanent solution is to place old age pensions on a straight insurance basis, and to institute a system of contributory old age pensions to which people will be obliged to contribute. I do not like the minister's idea of having a social service tax for this purpose of old age

Supply-Health and Welfare
pensions, or for this or that other purpose. I think it should be on a straight insurance principle, and on a sound actuarial basis. As soon as a man comes into employment he would start to make payments to the old age pension fund, or the old age pension insurance scheme, whatever you wish to call it. Then, upon reaching the age provided under the scheme-and that could be made anything within reason-he would receive an amount in proportion to what he has paid in. In my opinion that is the only way we can satisfactorily solve the old age pension situation.
Has the government given any thought to setting up an old age pension insurance scheme along these lines?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext: A great deal of consideration has been given to that and to all other old age pension plans. It will continue to be given. Regarding the plan such as the hon. member has suggested it must be remembered that in a country like Canada about half the population are self-employed. This makes it very difficult to relate a payment directly to the amount to be received. Further, if that is done you still have to provide pensions for those needing them but who have not contributed. So that you have to have a means-test plan supplementing the other. We have reached the conclusion that, having 'regard to the particular situation in Canada, the most effective and the fairest way is the one I have described, and that is, cover part of the cost with a tax, which we thought might amount to three per cent, and which would be paid by everyone able to pay.

maintopic: STAFF DISTRIBUTION BY PERMANENTS AND TEMPORARIES AS AT MARCH 31, 1946.
speechtext:
One of my chief objections against a contributory scheme is that those who need pensions most are, generally speaking. unable to contribute, and therefore not in a position to benefit. I have in mind especially the workers in primary industry.
I recall that before the war we in this group were urging the payment of a pension of $50 a month at the age of sixty, and that in those days we were told time and again that the government could not possibly afford to pay out so much money, and that it had not any money for that purpose. I also recall that within six weeks of the declaration of war the government had the chartered banks create for its use over $200 million. I would remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare that when that $200 million was created for purposes of the war, it was not printing press money. That amount of money was created by the chartered banks, without the printing of a single dollar; it was cheque book money.
Let me again remind the minister that we would never have had the war effort we did
have, had it not been for the fact that four billions of dollars in new money was created- and it was created by the banking business, without printing. It was cheque money.
Mr. Graham Towers warns us that in the very near future we shall be passing into a time where there will be a lack of effective markets. I would suggest that one of the best ways we can create in Canada good markets would be to help the old age pensioners by paying them an adequate amount of money, so that they can buy goods. As the governor of the Bank of Canada has pointed out, one of our great troubles in the future will not be the fact that we cannot produce, but the fact that we have produced goods which we cannot sell.
The minister may suggest that we shall have goods but we shall not have the money. I ask him this question: Did he ever once during the war hear it said that we could not have a battleship, or could not have aircraft, or could not have material for the army because we did not have the money? He knows very well that the only thing that hindered the war effort was the mere matter of production of goods and services. Where those goods and services were available, money was made available to buy them.
What did we fight for? We were told that we were fighting for a new social order. Surely the old age pensioner should have a new social order. If we can create money to win the war to achieve a new social order, then I say that we should be able to create money to enjoy the benefits of that social order after we have won the war. Any government which suggests for one minute that it cannot get money for that purpose is fooling the people of the country, and the people will not be fooled. The people are not going to be willing in future to be told that we are going to have to do without things of this kind because the government is still hanging on to some old-fashioned money system which has no relationship whatsoever to the productive capacity of the country.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 57S.	Treatment of Canadian fishermen and seamen, $15,000'.

In connection with this item, I should like to refer to part V, sections 304 to 308 inclusive of the Canada Shipping Act, with particular reference to section 305.

Supply-Health and Welfare
This section discriminates against the treatment of certain seamen engaged in coastal traffic, especially those sailing along the coast of British Columbia and between ports in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Section 305 reads:
(1) There shall be levied and collected on every ship arriving in any port in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island. British Columbia or in any port on Hudson bay or James bay in the provinces of Manitoba or Ontario, hereinafter called ''the provinces," a duty of two cents for every ton which such ship measures, register tonnage, unless
(a)	the ship is engaged in the coasting trade of Canada and arrives at any port in any of the said provinces from any other port in the same province, or arrives at any port in the province of Quebec from any port m the province of Ontario, and has not during the calendar year made a payment on account of such duty; or unless
(b)	the ship is a ship which came from a place out of Canada and has paid duty on the same voyage in a previous port of call in' Canada.
Under that section seamen engaged along the coast of British Columbia or in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec do not have the benefit of hospital treatment which is provided for seamen on ships plying between different provinces. In British Columbia we would like to see the act extended so that seamen engaged in the coastal trade in that province could receive treatment. These exceptions should be done away with. During the war, part V of the act, principally section 308, was amended by order in council P.C. 164/6991, but this amendment has since been rescinded on the pretence that it was just a war measure. That order reads:
Tree medical treatment and care may be provided by the Department of Pensions .and National Health for any sick or disabled seaman not entitled thereto under the provisions of part V of the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, if such seaman is suffering from sickness or disability with respect to which entitlement to a pension has not been conceded under any existing law, where such sickness arose or disability was incurred on a ship of Canadian registry, or is a seaman of Canadian nationality serving on a ship of other than Canadian registry, while the ship was operating in such waters as may be determined by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, on the advice of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, to be particularly liable to enemy attack.
Surely these social services should have been maintained on the books in peace time. If they were desirable in time of war, surely they should be maintained in time of peace. Under the Canada Shipping Act, if a man is taken seriously ill or meets with an accident on a vessel and is hospitalized at the first port of call and should later be released as fit to be returned home, he is then thrown on the mercy of his Britannic Majesty's consul,
who sees that he is returned to his home port. He may even travel home in the company of some cattle that are being shipped in the same direction. If, on arrival at his home port, the man should still require medical attention he is denied such attention under the terms of the act for the reason that he did not return on the same vessel. In other words, a man must avoid treatment in a foreign port, even if he is dying, to assure himself of medical attention when and if he is lucky enough to survive and reach his home port on his own vessel. By the same token, if a man were injured or suffered illness through shipwreck he would have to refuse being rescued and endeavour to salvage his vessel and bring it back with him in order to receive the medical attention he would require. This is covered in part V, section 308, and, to say the least, is nonsensical.
In this connection, dealing with the health of seamen I should like to deal with section 288. This section allows for treatment of venereal disease in any Canadian port whether a man is ashore or on shipboard, but if a man on a Canadian vessel contracts venereal disease in a port other than a Canadian one he is responsible fo" his own treatment. In this connection, it is to be noted that Canadian vessels are the only vessels in the world to-day where this is still the practice. Even Great Britain changed the clause in the British Shipping Act, and to-day treats venereal disease in the classification of general illness. On November 10, 1943, four members of the crew of the sailing vessel, the City oj Albcrni, contracted venereal disease while their vessel lay in the port of Valparaiso. They were charged with deductions from their wages for medical expenses incurred in treatment of the disease. It was the contention of their union representatives that, in view of the fact that all maritime nations do accept the treatment of venereal disease the same as any other illness, the cost of treatment should not be charged to the men. However, they were charged under the "wilful" clause of the act. The Department of Transport in this case referred the union to the courts. Rather than referring the union to the courts a little action by the government in line with other maritime nations would save a great deal of unnecessary suffering and needless expense to the individuals concerned.
This is a matter of vital concern to the seamen of Canada's merchant marine, and with all the talk we hear from the present government as to their interest in social welfare, why cannot they maintain the order in council which they passed during the war?
Supply-Health and Welfare

It is part and parcel of the general set-up of other maritime nations. It was regarded as very necessary in time of war. Some day we might want these seamen again, and they might not be willing to sail the boats unless conditions are changed. I am interested in this matter because I have worked on coastal boats and am a member of the international seafarers' union. I should like to see these men given the service they deserve.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Similar representations
have been made by other members from time to time, in addition to those made to-night by the hon. member for Skeena. He has said that section 303 of the Canada Shipping Act discriminates against this class of seamen. He also said that other countries had more generous provisions with- regard to these seamen. My information is that no country provides the kind of coverage that he mentions.
The situation, as I understand it, is this. Under section 305 of the Canada Shipping Act, which in one form or another has been in effect for a great number of years, owners of ships engaged in international or interprovincial trade are required to pay a certain fee into the sick mariners' fund. That fee is two cents per ton. Out of the fund the federal government, acting through the Department of National Health and Welfare, provides services to sick mariners. This came up in connection with the vote under item 210, arid at that time I think some figures were put on Hansard. It runs into a very considerable sum of money. In the fiscal year 1944-45 the revenue was $210,452.42 and the expenditure *vas $303,747.58. But, generally speaking, over the years, the expenditure is just about offset by the revenue. This measure is arrived at by international agreement. It provides protection for seamen who are covered by the terms of section 305: that is those who are engaged in international o>r interprovincial trade, not local trade.
The class of seamen whose cause has been so ably argued by the hon. member for Skeena are those who are engaged in trade within a single province. They are not ordinarily covered. It has been the view of the federal government and, I believe, all other governments of this and every country, since long before I had anything to do with this administration, that the responsibility for dealing with seamen in that class was a matter of local jurisdiction, in this case a matter within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Indeed provision for the purpose is, I understand, made in some if not in all of the provinces under the workmen's compensation acts. Further, I am informed that in the

case of some of the vessels in this class there is a requirement by the Department of Transport that they do secure protection under the workmen's compensation act. But that comes under the Department of Transport and I am not familiar with the details. There is no discrimination in any sense. The coasting vessels, which are the vessels which are worked by this class of seamen, do not make any contribution. They do not come within the legislation. It has been the view that if there should be protection for that class of seamen operating within the ordinary limits of a province, it should be provided by the workmen's compensation law of the province. I might point out that, whereas the situation regarding men engaged on deep-sea work is as I have described it, that is, year in and year out the costs are just about met by the revenue. The situation is quite different with regard to the vessels which carry on an interprovincial trade as opposed to an international trade. In 1938, which was a normal peacetime year, coastal vessels covered having a crew membership of 8,652 paid $7,984.98, and treatment was given to the amount of $56,260.16. In 1944, this class of vessel, with a crew membership of 9,547, paid out $9,133.90, while treatment costing $59,742.97 was given.

I should like to say a few words in support of some of the points raised by the bon. member for Skeena. The minister may remember that I discussed this matter with him last year. I first took it up with the Minister of Transport, and had prepared an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act which I thought would meet the situation. The men, and the women too, I imagine, who work on coastal ships in British Columbia feel that they are being discriminated against. The department is not necessarily to blame for this, because it is only administering the sick mariners' fund according to the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is right.

-which provides that only vessels which ply between international ports or ports between two different provinces pay dues. But here is the sort of situation which arises. A ship crosses from Prince Edward Island to New Brunswick, or from New Brunswick to Prince Edward Island, a distance of nine or ten miles, and because of that, contributions are made to the sick mariners' fund and the crews are looked after in case of illness; or in British Columbia a boat goes from Vancouver to Seattle or from Victoria to Seattle and the crews of those boats are covered by the benefits of the sick mariners' fund. But take a much longer sea

Slipply-Health and Welfare
journey, from Prince Rupert to Vancouver, and ships operated by the same company are not covered. So the employees of these ships feel that they are being discriminated against. The minister mentioned that they are covered by workmen's compensation. That is quite true, but the workmen's compensation fund covers them only in case of accident, not in case of illness.
Let me take two cases. An employee on a Canadian Pacific boat plying between Vancouver and Seattle becomes ill with appendicitis; he is taken to a hospital and his hospital bills are taken care of out of the sick mariners' fund. A person on a sister ship running between Victoria and Vancouver, or between Prince Rupert and Vancouver-much longer distances-takes sick with appendicitis, goes to hospital, and has to pay his own hospital and doctor bills, and if he is unable to pay them while he is in the hospital he comes out with a debt which he must discharge. What is required, I submit, is an amendment to section 305, I think it is, of the Canada Shipping Act, so that this provision will be applicable to ships plying between different ports in the same province as well as to ships plying between ports in different provinces. It seems to me that the remedy is very simple. I do not see that any provincial rights enter into the matter; I do not believe any province would object to such an amendment. I ask the minister again, as I did eight or nine months ago, to take the matter under consideration and see if something cannot be done to obviate this most illogical situation.
I was rising to speak on the same subject. I do not profess to have anything like the detailed knowledge which the hon. member for Skeena has.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It has just occurred to me that the hon. member is going to discuss an amendment of the act. This is hardly the time to discuss it. I do not know whether the act comes within the purview of the Department of National Health and Welfare, but, if not, it would not be pertinent to the vote under consideration. The committee is considering item 573, treatment of Canadian fishermen and seamen, $15,000, and the discussion should be confined to the purpose for which that money is used.

I wonder if, before the hon. member for Nanaimo resumes his remarks, I might speak to that point of order. Ip a certain sense, I believe, Mr. Chairman, your point of order is well taken, because we have passed the item dealing with the sick mariners' fund. But the sick mariners' fund is under a section of the Canada Shipping Act which comes
under the administration of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I thought at one time that it was under the administration of the Minister of Transport, but that particular section, 305, of the Canada Shipping Act is under the administration of this department, and it can be discussed. There has been some discussion on it, and I do not want to speak to it further, but I suggest that the hon. member for Nanaimo be permitted to make his particular point, because the matter is one of importance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion has gone on at some considerable length. I was under the impression that the administration of the act came under a different department.
No; it comes under the Department of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think we should allow the hon. member for Nanaimo to make his remarks, and then we might coniine the discussion to the vote under consideration.

I just want to add my support to what the hon. member for Skeena said, because the same problem has been brought up by the fishermen and the seamen in my own constituency. We have those boats which have been referred to as going from Vancouver to Victoria, in which perhaps a seaman who is taken ill cannot receive treatment on that tour. If, however, he goes on from Victoria to Seattle, on the same boat,, on the same trip, I believe, although I am not positive, that he can receive the treatment. But there are a number of fishermen operating out from Nanaimo and other ports in my constituency who go out into the deep seas, who continue fishing for a long time and then return to these ports in British Columbia and there is a feeling amongst them that there is some discrimination and that it is not possible for them to receive some of the benefits which they believe the fishermen on the maritime seaboard receive if they go out from one of the ports of New Brunswick and happen to put back into a port in Nova Scotia.

Why is the money needed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Under the agreement we are continuing to pay the cost of operating the chlorination plants until December 31,1946.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Demobilization and Reconversion - National Health and Welfare-
578.	Greater Vancouver, North Vancouver city and district, $35,000.
Knowing now that chlor-amination and chlorination mean the same thing -

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Perhaps I should explain that. The additional syllable is introduced to indicate the addition of a very small portion of ammonia. It is only an infinitesimal part.

I imagine the amount of ammonia that is added does not affect the matter to such an extent that I may not raise the point which I am about to discuss. Perhaps there was a professor mixed up in these estimates. My understanding is that the chlorination of the water supply of Vancouver has been discontinued. As a matter of fact, and as a matter of history, the chlorination of the water supply of Vancouver was imposed upon the residents and the municipal authorities of that city after a strenuous fight. I do not know whether the members of this committee know it, but the water supply of Vancouver is so pure that when you chlorinate it you really contaminate it. That indeed was proven by this fact that there was a fish hatchery that was supplied by water from our water supply, and after the dominion authorities, acting in their wisdom, purified our water by chlorinating it, it killed all the fish in the hatchery'. So we had the peculiar situation that the water was not pure unless it killed fish. The war being over, however, I understand that the municipal fathers in Vancouver have had the chlorination stopped. I do not see, therefore, what this vote is for. They have stopped the chlorination of the water, and I understand they are pasteurizing the milk instead. That is actually the situation, and I see no reason in the world why there should be $35,000 in the estimates to contaminate the water supply of the city of Vancouver.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. gentleman expects me to enter into a discussion of the fundamental situation in connection with the water supply in Vancouver. That can be done by other people and the two sides of the question have been vociferously put forward by people on the spot. With regard to the question the hon. member asks, the situation is that the votes for these three chlorination plants are lumped together, and until an agreement is reached with each of the three municipalities we might be liable, under the agreement we entered into to chlorinate the water for them, to pay any expenses up to the end of the war. But if the agreements are signed, as we expect they will be, then the obligation with regard to Vancouver will terminate from March 31, 1946, and the amount provided in the vote in connection with Vancouver will not be needed. But we should have the item there,

Private Bills
because there is the possibility of the obligation running until the formal termination of hostilities.

One other question. I understand that the chlorinating machinery- I presume that is the right term-has been turned over to War Assets Corporation and that it is no longer there. If the machinery for the chlorinating is not there, then certainly the agreement has definitely come to an end as far as Vancouver is concerned and there is no need for this item.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The machinery is still there.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We have made very good progress and concluded all the items of this department except those that come under a separate branch for the film board, and since it is ten minutes to eleven o'clock and a very hot night I wonder if it might not meet the views of the committee to rise now.

I do not like to resist the suggestion that the committee should rise after a hard day's work, but there is a question relating to the estimates which I asked the minister on a previous occasion and which has not yet been answered. It will be found at page 2584 of Hansard of June 17. I said then:
Would the minister give figures indicating the incidence of venereal disease within, say, the last two years, to establish trends, including both the civilian population and the armed services?
The minister in reply, after making an explanatory statement, said he had figures for 1943-44 but could not lay his hands on them at the time. Will he kindly put those figures on Hansard, as well as the figures for 1945 if he has them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: In doing that, I think I should recall to members of the committee the warning I gave about the use of figures with regard to venereal disease. The greater degree of cooperation you get, the greater the amount of reporting of the figures by the provincial and municipal authorities and by doctors, the higher the apparent rate of venereal disease. The figures, therefore, must be read cautiously and by those who are familiar with them in order to derive their true meaning. The total venereal disease in 1944 as reported by provincial health departments to the dominion bureau of statistics was 38,772 cases; in 1945, 40,527 cases. The total syphilis for 1944, was 16,475 cases; in 1945, 15,278 cases.
That is a reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes. In 1944, the number of cases of gonorrhoea was 22,282; in 1945, 25,237. In 1944, other venereal diseases amounted to fifteen cases; in 1945, twelve cases.
Has the minister the figures for 1943 as well?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
No. The reporting began only in 1943, in accordance with arrangements worked out in 1943, and I have not the figures. I do not think there are figures. If there are I shall make sure that the hon. member gets them.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. St. Laurent the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m., until Tuesday July 2.
